replace_subtopics.title: Headers and authentication
replace_subtopics.body:
Headers are name and value pairs sent before the body. Content-Type says what format the body is in, usually application/json. Accept says what format you want back. User-Agent names your client.

The most important header is Authorization. APIs need to know who is calling, so you send a secret. An API key is a long random string the provider gives you. A bearer token is a string you send as 'Authorization: Bearer <token>', and it often expires after an hour or so. OAuth 2.0 is a common standard for obtaining such tokens: your program trades a client id and client secret, or a user's approval, for a short-lived access token.

Tokens are passwords. Keep them in environment variables or a secret manager, never in code, and never paste them into tickets or chat.

Two older schemes are still common on enterprise systems such as ERPs and on-premise tools. HTTP Basic auth sends a username and password on every call. The client joins them as user:password, encodes that with base64 and sends 'Authorization: Basic <encoded>'. Base64 is only an encoding, not encryption: anyone who sees the header can decode it in one line. So Basic auth is acceptable only over HTTPS, with a dedicated service account, never a person's own login. In requests you pass auth=(user, password) and the library builds the header.

Some APIs want the API key in the query string, as in ?key=abc123. It works, but URLs get written to proxy logs, server access logs and browser history, so the key leaks more easily than a header does. Use a header if the API accepts one. If it does not, keep the full URL out of your own logs.
replace_subtopics.example: A hospital's scheduling system uses OAuth 2.0 client credentials. Your service first POSTs its client id and secret to the token endpoint and receives an access token valid for 3600 seconds. Every API call then sends that token in the Authorization header. After an hour, calls start returning 401 Unauthorized, which is your signal to fetch a new token and try again. The same hospital also runs an older on-premise pharmacy system that only supports Basic auth. You ask their IT team for a service account called svc_fde with read-only rights, store the password in the secret manager, and call it over HTTPS with auth=(user, password). A mapping API they license takes ?key= in the URL, so your logger prints only the path, never the query string.
replace_subtopics.code:
import os, requests

# 1. Exchange client credentials for a short-lived access token
tok = requests.post(
    "https://auth.clinic-example.org/oauth/token",
    data={"grant_type": "client_credentials",
          "client_id": os.environ["CLIENT_ID"],
          "client_secret": os.environ["CLIENT_SECRET"]},
    timeout=10,
).json()
access_token = tok["access_token"]        # expires_in is often 3600

# 2. Send it as a bearer token on every call
r = requests.get(
    "https://api.clinic-example.org/v1/appointments",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {access_token}",
             "Accept": "application/json"},
    timeout=10,
)
print(r.status_code)

# 3. HTTP Basic auth: "user:password" base64-encoded, sent on every call.
#    Base64 is NOT encryption, so only ever use it over HTTPS.
req = requests.Request("GET", "https://erp.example-legacy.com/api/items",
                       auth=("svc_fde", "s3cret")).prepare()
print(req.headers["Authorization"])   # Basic c3ZjX2ZkZTpzM2NyZXQ=

# 4. API key as a query parameter (some older APIs insist on this)
req = requests.Request("GET", "https://geo.example-maps.com/v1/geocode",
                       params={"q": "Leeds", "key": "KEY123"}).prepare()
print(req.url)   # https://geo.example-maps.com/v1/geocode?q=Leeds&key=KEY123
# That full URL can end up in proxy and server logs: never log it as it is.

replace_subtopics.title: Status codes tell you what happened
replace_subtopics.body:
Every response starts with a three-digit status code. The first digit is the class. 2xx means success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content. 3xx means the resource moved and you should follow a redirect. 4xx means the client, meaning you, did something wrong. 5xx means the server had a problem.

The 4xx codes you will see most are 400 Bad Request (malformed input), 401 Unauthorized (missing or expired credentials), 403 Forbidden (valid credentials without permission), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable (the data failed validation) and 429 Too Many Requests (you hit a rate limit). The 5xx codes are 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable and 504 Gateway Timeout.

The class tells you what to do next. Retrying a 400 will fail forever because the request itself is wrong. Retrying a 429 or 503 after a pause often succeeds. A 429 response frequently includes a Retry-After header saying how many seconds to wait.

3xx redirects need a closer look. requests follows them automatically, and r.history lists the hops. Two surprises catch people. First, when the redirect points to a different host, requests drops your Authorization header on purpose so your token is not sent to a stranger, and the new host then answers 401. The fix is to call the final URL directly. Second, a 301 or 302 in reply to a POST is usually retried as a GET without the body; only 307 and 308 keep the method and body. Two more 4xx codes to know: 405 Method Not Allowed (for example POST to a read-only path) and 413 Payload Too Large (your upload or batch is over the server's size limit, so send smaller pieces).

Many APIs also tell you how close you are to the rate limit on every response, not just on the 429. Common headers are X-RateLimit-Limit (calls allowed per window), X-RateLimit-Remaining (calls left) and X-RateLimit-Reset (when the window resets). A newer standard uses RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset. Check the docs for the Reset unit: some APIs send a Unix time, others a number of seconds from now. A polite client slows down when Remaining gets low, instead of waiting to be blocked.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer's claims API returns a mix of responses during a nightly sync: 9,850 calls get 200, 120 get 429, 25 get 503 and 5 get 422. The 429s and 503s are temporary and should be retried with a wait. The 5 calls with 422 have a body saying 'policy_number must be 10 digits'. Those are data problems. Retrying will not help, so you log them and report the bad records to the customer. Later the same insurer moves the API from api.insurer-example.com to api2.insurer-example.com with a 301 redirect. Your GETs suddenly return 401 even though the token is valid, because requests removed the Authorization header when the host changed. Printing r.history shows the 301 hop, and pointing the client at api2 fixes it. You also read X-RateLimit-Remaining and pause when it drops below 5, and the 429 count falls from 120 to zero.

replace_subtopics.title: JSON bodies in and out
replace_subtopics.body:
JSON is text with a few building blocks: objects in curly braces holding named fields, arrays in square brackets holding lists, strings in double quotes, numbers, true, false and null. Python's json module and the requests library convert JSON objects to dicts and arrays to lists.

When you send data, pass it with json= in requests. The library serialises the dict to JSON text and sets the Content-Type header for you. When you receive data, call r.json() to parse the body.

Never assume every field is present. Real APIs omit empty fields, return null, or change a number into a string between versions. Use .get() with a default, or validate the response with a schema library such as Pydantic.

json= is not the only body type. data= sends a form-encoded body (Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded, text like grant_type=client_credentials&scope=read). That is what the OAuth token call in the headers section uses, because token endpoints expect a form, not JSON. files= sends a multipart body (multipart/form-data), which is how you upload a PDF, image or CSV. Each file part has a field name, a filename, the file bytes and a content type, and you can send normal form fields next to it with data=. Always open files in binary mode, 'rb'.

Some values need deliberate parsing. Dates arrive as ISO 8601 strings such as 2026-03-01T09:30:00Z. The Z or an offset like +01:00 says which timezone; a string without one is ambiguous, so ask the customer what it means before you compare it with other times. Money is often sent as a string such as "19.99" so that it is not rounded; read it with Decimal, never float. Very large ids are sometimes sent as strings too, because JavaScript loses precision above 2 to the power 53. Keep those as strings.
replace_subtopics.example: A logistics company's shipment API returns {"id": "SHP-77", "weight_kg": 12.5, "delivered_at": null, "items": [{"sku": "A1", "qty": 3}]}. In Python that becomes a dict whose items field is a list of dicts. delivered_at is None because the parcel is still in transit, so code that calls a date method on it would crash. Checking for None first avoids the crash. A claims team wants you to upload their daily CSV to an insurer's intake API. The API takes multipart with a field named file plus a batch field, so you send files= and data= together. The response contains "created_at": "2026-03-01T09:30:00Z" and "total": "19.99". You parse the date as a UTC datetime and the total as Decimal('19.99'), so three claims sum to exactly 59.97.

import requests

# Send JSON: requests serialises the dict and sets Content-Type
r = requests.post("https://api.shipco-example.com/v1/shipments",
                  json={"sku": "A1", "qty": 3, "to": "Leeds"},
                  headers={"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"},
                  timeout=10)
shipment = r.json()                 # JSON text -> dict

# Read defensively: fields may be missing or null
weight = shipment.get("weight_kg", 0.0)
delivered = shipment.get("delivered_at")    # None if in transit
if delivered is None:
    print(shipment["id"], "still in transit")
for item in shipment.get("items", []):
    print(item["sku"], item["qty"])

import io, json
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from decimal import Decimal

# Form-encoded body (data=): what OAuth token endpoints and old web forms expect
req = requests.Request("POST", "https://auth.example.org/token",
                       data={"grant_type": "client_credentials", "scope": "read"}).prepare()
print(req.headers["Content-Type"])  # application/x-www-form-urlencoded
print(req.body)                     # grant_type=client_credentials&scope=read

# Multipart upload (files=): sending a CSV or PDF
csv_file = io.BytesIO(b"claim_id,amount\nC-1,120.50\n")   # normally open("claims.csv", "rb")
req = requests.Request("POST", "https://api.insure-example.com/v1/uploads",
                       files={"file": ("claims.csv", csv_file, "text/csv")},
                       data={"batch": "2026-09"}).prepare()
print(req.headers["Content-Type"][:30])  # multipart/form-data; boundary=

# Dates, money and big ids: parse them on purpose
order = json.loads('{"id": "90071992547409931", "total": "19.99", '
                   '"created_at": "2026-03-01T09:30:00Z", "local": "2026-03-01T09:30:00"}')
created = datetime.fromisoformat(order["created_at"])   # Python 3.11+ accepts the Z
print(created.tzinfo)                                   # UTC
local = datetime.fromisoformat(order["local"])
print(local.tzinfo)                                     # None: ask which timezone it means
local = local.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)              # only after the customer confirms UTC
total = Decimal(order["total"])                         # exact, unlike float
print(total * 3)                                        # 59.97
print(0.1 + 0.2)                                        # 0.30000000000000004
print(json.loads('{"total": 19.99}', parse_float=Decimal))  # {'total': Decimal('19.99')}

replace_subtopics.title: Pagination: getting all the data
replace_subtopics.body:
An API will not return a million records in one response. It returns a page, perhaps 100 items, plus a way to ask for the next page. You loop until there are no more pages.

There are three common styles. Offset pagination uses ?offset=200&limit=100. It is simple, but if rows are inserted while you page, items shift and you can skip or repeat some. Cursor pagination returns an opaque token like next_cursor that you send back, and it stays stable while data changes. Link-header pagination puts the URL of the next page in a Link response header; requests exposes it as r.links.

Always check the API documentation for which style is used and what the maximum page size is. Larger pages mean fewer calls and less risk of hitting rate limits.

The code below uses requests.Session instead of calling requests.get directly. A session keeps the network connection to the server open between calls (keep-alive), so page 2 onwards skips the TCP and TLS handshake. On a pull of hundreds of pages that is noticeably faster, and it puts less load on the customer's server. A session also holds default headers, such as Authorization, that it adds to every call, plus cookies. Create one session per API and reuse it.

httpx is a newer library with almost the same interface. httpx.Client plays the role of a session. httpx.AsyncClient does the same with async and await, so you can send several requests at once, for example to fetch 50 accounts in parallel. Cursor pages must still be fetched one after another, because each page tells you the next cursor, but independent calls can overlap. Keep the parallelism small, such as 5 at a time, so you stay under the rate limit.
replace_subtopics.example: A SaaS CRM holds 48,200 contacts and returns at most 200 per page with a cursor. Your loop makes 242 calls. The last response has next_cursor set to null, which ends the loop. Had you stopped after the first call, your report would have claimed the customer has 200 contacts, a mistake that would surface in the first demo. Pulling the 48,200 contacts with a plain requests.get per page took 97 seconds; the same loop with one Session took 61 seconds because the TLS handshake happened once instead of 242 times. For the account details, one call per account, an httpx.AsyncClient with 5 requests in flight cut a 4 minute job to under a minute.
replace_subtopics.code:
import requests

def fetch_all_contacts(session, base_url):
    contacts, cursor = [], None
    while True:
        params = {"limit": 200}
        if cursor:
            params["cursor"] = cursor
        r = session.get(f"{base_url}/v1/contacts", params=params, timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()
        page = r.json()
        contacts.extend(page["items"])
        cursor = page.get("next_cursor")
        if not cursor:                     # last page reached
            return contacts

s = requests.Session()                      # reuses the connection
s.headers["Authorization"] = "Bearer TOKEN"
print(len(fetch_all_contacts(s, "https://api.crm-example.com")))

import asyncio, httpx

# httpx.Client is the httpx version of requests.Session
with httpx.Client(base_url="https://api.crm-example.com",
                  headers={"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"}, timeout=10) as client:
    r = client.get("/v1/contacts", params={"limit": 200})

# httpx.AsyncClient: independent calls in parallel, at most 5 at a time
async def fetch_accounts(ids):
    limit = asyncio.Semaphore(5)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="https://api.crm-example.com",
                                 headers={"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"},
                                 timeout=10) as client:
        async def one(i):
            async with limit:
                r = await client.get(f"/v1/accounts/{i}")
                r.raise_for_status()
                return r.json()
        return await asyncio.gather(*(one(i) for i in ids))

replace_subtopics.title: Debugging with curl first
replace_subtopics.body:
curl is a command-line tool that sends HTTP requests. It is installed on almost every machine, including locked-down customer servers where you cannot install Python packages. Reproducing a failing call with curl removes your own code from the question.

Useful flags: -X sets the method, -H adds a header, -d sends a body, -i prints response headers, -v prints the whole conversation including TLS details, and -w can print the status code and timing. If curl works and your code fails, the bug is in your code. If curl fails the same way, the problem is the token, the network, or the API itself.

When you share a curl command in a ticket, replace the token with a placeholder first.

curl is not the only option. HTTPie is a command-line client with shorter syntax and coloured output. Postman and Bruno are desktop apps where you save requests in collections, keep variables such as base_url and token per environment, and share them with teammates. Bruno stores collections as plain files you can commit to git, which suits customers that do not allow cloud tools. Check the customer's policy before you put their tokens into any desktop tool that syncs to the cloud.

The fastest way to reproduce a call the customer's own web app makes is Copy as cURL. Open the browser developer tools (F12), go to the Network tab, do the action in the app, right-click the request and choose Copy, then Copy as cURL. You get the exact URL, headers, cookies and body, ready to paste into a terminal or import into Postman or Bruno. That command contains the user's session cookie or token, so treat it like a password: remove those headers before you save or share it.
replace_subtopics.example: A manufacturer's parts API times out from your pipeline. From the same server you run curl with -w to print the time. It takes 29 seconds and returns 504 Gateway Timeout, while the same call for a smaller date range returns in 0.4 seconds with 200. That tells you the API struggles with large queries, so you split the pull into daily ranges. A support agent at a logistics firm says the 'export shipments' button fails for March only. You watch them click it with developer tools open, copy the failing request as cURL, and run it yourself. It returns 413 Payload Too Large, so the export needs to be split by week. The whole diagnosis took ten minutes and no code.
replace_subtopics.code:
# Show response headers (-i) and the status code and time (-w)
curl -s -i \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PARTS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -w "\nstatus=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}s\n" \
  "https://api.parts-example.com/v1/parts?updated_since=2026-01-01"

# Send a JSON body with POST
curl -s -X POST "https://api.parts-example.com/v1/parts" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $PARTS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"part_no": "BRK-220", "qty": 40}'

# The same GET with HTTPie: == adds a query parameter, Name:value adds a header
http GET "https://api.parts-example.com/v1/parts" updated_since==2026-01-01 \
  "Authorization:Bearer $PARTS_TOKEN"

# A request pasted from the browser with Copy as cURL (trimmed).
# Delete the cookie and authorization lines before saving or sharing it.
curl 'https://app.shipco-example.com/api/exports?month=2026-03' \
  -H 'accept: application/json' \
  -H 'cookie: session=REDACTED'

add_glossary: Basic auth
An old authentication scheme that sends base64 of user:password in the Authorization header; safe only over HTTPS.
Form-encoded body
A request body like a=1&b=2 with Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded, sent with data= in requests.
Multipart upload
A request body of several parts, used to upload files, with Content-Type multipart/form-data, sent with files= in requests.
Redirect
A 3xx response that tells the client to repeat the request at another URL given in the Location header.
Keep-alive
Reusing one open network connection for many requests, which a requests.Session or httpx.Client does for you.
Rate-limit headers
Response headers such as X-RateLimit-Remaining that say how many calls you have left before you get 429.
Copy as cURL
A browser developer tools option that copies any network request as a ready-to-run curl command.
ISO 8601
The standard text format for dates and times, such as 2026-03-01T09:30:00Z, where Z means UTC.

add_subtopics.title: Rebase versus merge, and keeping a branch up to date
add_subtopics.body:
While you work on a branch, main keeps moving as other people merge. There are two ways to bring those new commits into your branch.

git merge origin/main adds one new merge commit that joins the two lines of history. Nothing that already exists changes, so it is always safe, but a long-lived branch collects many merge commits and the history looks like a tangle.

git rebase origin/main takes your commits off, moves your branch to the tip of main, and replays your commits on top, one by one. The result is a straight line, as if you had started your work today. The catch is that every replayed commit gets a new id. That is what rewriting history means. If you already pushed the branch, you must push again with git push --force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite commits you have not seen.

The golden rule: only rebase a branch that nobody else works on. Never rebase main or a branch a teammate has pulled, because their copy still has the old commit ids and Git will think the work diverged. During a rebase a conflict stops at each commit. Fix the file, git add it, then git rebase --continue, or git rebase --abort to go back.

On GitHub and GitLab the merge button offers three options. Create a merge commit keeps every commit plus a merge commit. Squash and merge turns the whole pull request into one commit on main, which keeps main tidy and easy to revert. Rebase and merge replays each commit onto main without a merge commit. Many customer teams pick squash; follow whatever the repo already does.
add_subtopics.example: At a logistics customer your branch feat/eta-model is 12 commits behind main after a week. The team uses squash merges and a linear history, so you run git fetch and git rebase origin/main. One commit conflicts in features.py; you fix it, git add, git rebase --continue, run the tests and push with --force-with-lease. The pull request now shows only your 4 commits on top of today's main.
add_subtopics.code:
git fetch origin

# Option 1: merge (safe, adds a merge commit)
git merge origin/main

# Option 2: rebase (straight history, rewrites YOUR branch's commit ids)
git rebase origin/main
# CONFLICT in features.py -> edit the file, then:
git add features.py
git rebase --continue          # or: git rebase --abort to undo the whole rebase

pytest -q
git push --force-with-lease    # needed after a rebase; refuses to erase others' work

git log --oneline --graph -8   # see the shape of the history

# Never: git rebase on main, or on a branch someone else has pulled.

add_subtopics.title: Rescue tools: stash, reflog, cherry-pick and blame
add_subtopics.body:
Four commands get you out of everyday trouble.

git stash puts your uncommitted edits on a shelf and gives you a clean working tree. Use it when someone asks for an urgent fix while you are halfway through something else. git stash list shows the shelf, and git stash pop brings the latest edits back and removes them from the shelf. Add -u to include untracked files.

git reflog is Git's private diary of where HEAD has been on your machine: every commit, checkout, reset and rebase, for about 90 days. If a git reset --hard or a bad rebase seems to have deleted commits, they are almost always still there. Find the line from before the mistake in git reflog and move back to it with git reset --hard HEAD@{2} or create a branch there.

git cherry-pick <commit> copies one commit onto the branch you are on. The classic use is a hotfix that was merged to main and must also go to a release branch, without bringing everything else from main. Use -x so the new message records where it came from.

git blame -L 40,60 file.py shows, for each line in that range, the last commit that changed it, who made it and when. It is not about blaming a person. It gives you the commit and pull request that explain why a line looks the way it does. git log -S 'text' finds the commits that added or removed a piece of text.
add_subtopics.example: At a bank you are mid-way through a refactor when the customer reports a wrong fee rounding in production. You git stash, switch to main, fix it in one commit and merge it. The bank runs release/2.3 in production, so you cherry-pick -x that commit onto release/2.3. Back on your branch you git stash pop. Later a colleague runs git reset --hard by mistake and loses two commits; git reflog shows them at HEAD@{1}, and one command brings them back.
add_subtopics.code:
# Park unfinished work
git stash push -u -m "half-done refactor"
git stash list                  # stash@{0}: On feat/refactor: half-done refactor
# ...switch branches, fix, commit...
git stash pop                   # edits come back

# Recover 'lost' commits after a bad reset or rebase
git reflog | head -5
# 5f1eb45 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
# ac0e4b6 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add fee rounding test
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}       # or: git branch rescue ac0e4b6

# Copy one fix onto a release branch
git switch release/2.3
git cherry-pick -x 7d2e9f1      # message gets "(cherry picked from commit 7d2e9f1...)"

# Who last changed lines 40 to 60, and in which commit?
git blame -L 40,60 fees.py
git log -S "ROUND_HALF_UP" --oneline   # commits that added or removed this text

replace_subtopics.title: Branches and the remote
replace_subtopics.body:
A branch is a lightweight, movable name that points at a commit. main (older repos use master) is the shared branch that should always work. When you start a task, you create a new branch from main. Your commits move your branch forward and leave main alone.

A remote is a copy of the repository on a server, usually called origin, hosted on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or a customer's internal server. git push uploads your branch's commits to the remote. git pull downloads new commits from the remote and merges them into your current branch. git fetch downloads without merging, so you can look first.

Name branches after the work: fix/retry-429, feat/claims-export. Keep them short-lived, ideally merged within a few days, so they do not drift far from main.

Before your first commit on a new laptop, tell Git who you are with git config --global user.name and user.email. Use the email the customer's GitHub or GitLab knows, or your commits will not link to your account.

The remote also needs to know it is you. There are two common ways. With SSH you create a key pair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519, paste the public key (the .pub file) into your account settings, and clone with the git@ address. With HTTPS you clone the https:// address and use a personal access token (PAT) instead of a password when asked. Many customer GitLab servers only allow PATs, and some require single sign-on first. Give a token the smallest scope that works, such as read_repository and write_repository, and set an expiry date.

If clone hangs or fails with a certificate error inside a customer network, the traffic probably has to go through their proxy. git config --global http.proxy sets it, and the enterprise networking topic covers proxies and custom certificate bundles in detail.
replace_subtopics.example: Two FDEs work at an insurer. Ana creates feat/claims-export, and Ben creates fix/null-policy-dates, both from the same main commit. They commit and push independently for two days without affecting each other. Each branch gets its own pull request and review. On day one at an insurer you get a laptop and access to their self-hosted GitLab. SSH on port 22 is blocked by the firewall, so you create a PAT with read and write repository scopes and a 90 day expiry, set http.proxy to their proxy address, and clone over HTTPS. Your first push shows your name correctly because you set user.email to your insurer account address.

git switch main
git pull                              # get everyone's latest work
git switch -c feat/claims-export      # new branch from here

# ...edit, add, commit a few times...

git push -u origin feat/claims-export # first push sets upstream
git branch -a                         # list local and remote branches
git switch main                       # jump back; your branch is kept

# One-time setup on a new machine
git config --global user.name "Sam Rivera"
git config --global user.email "sam.rivera@insurer-example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Option A: SSH key
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "sam.rivera@insurer-example.com"
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub        # paste this into GitHub/GitLab > SSH keys
ssh -T git@gitlab.insurer-example.com
git clone git@gitlab.insurer-example.com:claims/pipeline.git

# Option B: HTTPS with a personal access token (PAT) as the password
git clone https://gitlab.insurer-example.com/claims/pipeline.git

# Behind a corporate proxy
git config --global http.proxy http://proxy.insurer-example.com:8080

replace_subtopics.title: Pull requests and code review
replace_subtopics.body:
A pull request (GitLab calls it a merge request) asks to merge one branch into another, usually into main. It shows the full diff, runs automated checks, and gives reviewers a place to comment on specific lines.

A good pull request does one thing. Its description says what changed, why, and how it was tested, and links the ticket. Keep it small enough to review in one sitting; a few hundred changed lines is a common rough ceiling.

Review is a conversation. Reviewers ask questions and suggest changes. You respond by pushing more commits to the same branch, and the pull request updates. When reviewers approve and CI is green, the pull request is merged. Many teams protect main so nothing can be pushed to it directly.

Commit messages are part of the review too. A common convention: a subject line of 50 characters or fewer, written as a command (Add retry on 429, not Added or Adding), no full stop, then a blank line and a body that explains why the change was needed, not just what. Put the ticket id in the subject or body so the change is traceable. Some teams use Conventional Commits, which start the subject with a type such as feat:, fix:, docs: or chore:, so tools can build changelogs automatically.

Sometimes you have read access to a customer's or an open source repo but no right to push branches. Then you use the fork-and-PR workflow: fork the repo into your own account, clone your fork, push your branch there, and open a pull request from your fork into the original. Add the original as a second remote called upstream so you can fetch its latest main.

When a set of merged changes is released, mark that exact commit with a tag. git tag -a v1.4.2 -m "..." creates an annotated tag with a message and author, and git push origin v1.4.2 shares it. GitHub and GitLab turn tags into releases with notes. The same version usually becomes the Docker image tag in the deploy topic, so anyone can map what is running back to the exact code.
replace_subtopics.example: Ben opens a pull request titled 'Treat empty policy start dates as missing, not 1970-01-01'. The description explains that 312 claims had empty dates that were being parsed as the Unix epoch, which skewed the age-of-policy feature. A customer engineer asks whether the model needs retraining. Ben answers, adds a test with an empty date, pushes, gets approval and merges. At a retailer, your fix commit reads 'fix: skip empty SKU rows in nightly load (RET-231)' with a body explaining that 1.2 percent of rows had blank SKUs and crashed the join. For their open source forecasting library, you have no push rights, so you fork it, push to your fork and open a pull request upstream. After the retailer's release, you tag the merged commit v1.4.2, and the pipeline image is built as forecasting:1.4.2.

## What
Treat empty policy_start_date as missing instead of 1970-01-01.

## Why
312 claims had empty dates parsed as the Unix epoch, which made
policy age look like 56 years and skewed the fraud model feature.

## How tested
- New unit test: test_empty_start_date_is_none
- Re-ran September backfill: 312 rows now null, 0 rows at 1970

## Follow-up
Feature table needs a rebuild; retraining ticket CLAIMS-418.

# A good commit message
git commit -m "fix: skip empty SKU rows in nightly load (RET-231)" \
           -m "1.2% of rows had blank SKUs and crashed the join on sku_id."

# Fork-and-PR when you cannot push to the original repo
git clone git@github.com:sam-rivera/forecast-lib.git     # your fork
cd forecast-lib
git remote add upstream https://github.com/forecast-org/forecast-lib.git
git fetch upstream
git switch -c fix/empty-sku upstream/main
# ...commit...
git push -u origin fix/empty-sku    # then open the PR from your fork on GitHub

# Tag a release
git tag -a v1.4.2 -m "Nightly load skips empty SKUs"
git push origin v1.4.2
git tag --list "v1.4*"

replace_subtopics.title: Undoing mistakes safely
replace_subtopics.body:
Git makes most mistakes recoverable. Before a commit, git restore discards edits to a file. git restore --staged unstages a file while keeping the edits.

After a commit that is already pushed and shared, use git revert. It creates a new commit that applies the opposite change. History stays intact, which matters on shared branches and in audited environments.

git reset and git push --force rewrite history. They are fine on your own unshared branch and dangerous on shared ones, because they can delete commits other people have. If a secret was ever committed, treat it as leaked even after you remove it, because it remains in history and in every clone. Rotate the secret.

git reset moves your branch to an earlier commit, and its flag decides what happens to the changes in the commits you step back over. --soft keeps them staged, ready to commit again. --mixed, the default, keeps them in your files but unstaged. --hard throws them away completely, along with any uncommitted edits, so double check with git status first. Use reset only on commits you have not pushed. If you made a typo in the last commit message or forgot a file, and have not pushed yet, git commit --amend replaces that last commit instead.

Prevention beats rescue. A .gitignore file at the root of the repo lists paths Git should never track: secrets, virtual environments, caches and data. .gitignore only affects untracked files. If a file is already committed, you must also run git rm --cached on it, which stops tracking it but leaves it on your disk. Then add a pre-commit hook with a secret scanner such as gitleaks or detect-secrets, so a commit that contains something that looks like a key is blocked before it is even created.
replace_subtopics.example: A deploy on Friday merges a change that breaks the nightly load at a retailer. Rather than debugging under pressure, you run git revert on the merge commit, open a pull request with the revert, get a quick approval and deploy. The pipeline is back to the previous behaviour in 15 minutes, and the original change can be fixed on Monday. You commit 'Add clams export' and notice the typo and a missing test file before pushing. git add tests/test_export.py and git commit --amend -m 'Add claims export' fixes both in one commit. Later you find that .env was committed a month ago. You add it to .gitignore, run git rm --cached .env, commit, and ask the customer to rotate the database password in it, because the old value is still in history.

git restore report.py            # discard unstaged edits
git restore --staged report.py   # unstage, keep the edits

git log --oneline -3
# 9c1e7aa Merge pull request #57 from feat/new-loader
# ...

git revert -m 1 9c1e7aa          # undo a merge commit (-m 1 keeps main's side)
git push                         # history keeps both the change and its undo

# .gitignore: stop secrets being committed in the first place
# .env
# *.pem

# git reset flavours (only on commits you have NOT pushed)
git reset --soft HEAD~1    # undo the last commit, keep its changes staged
git reset HEAD~1           # --mixed (default): keep changes, unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1    # undo the commit AND delete its changes

# Fix the last unpushed commit (message or a forgotten file)
git add tests/test_export.py
git commit --amend -m "Add claims export"

# A real .gitignore for a Python project
cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
.env
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.pem
*.key
data/
.pytest_cache/
EOF

# The file was already committed: stop tracking it, keep it on disk
git rm --cached .env
git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"
git status --short         # .env no longer listed

# Block secrets before they are committed (pre-commit framework)
# .pre-commit-config.yaml:
#   repos:
#     - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
#       rev: v8.24.2
#       hooks: [{id: gitleaks}]
pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install

add_glossary: Rebase
Replaying your branch's commits on top of another branch, which gives a straight history but new commit ids.
Force-with-lease
A safer force push that refuses to overwrite remote commits you have not fetched.
Squash merge
Merging a whole pull request as a single commit on main.
Stash
A shelf where Git keeps uncommitted edits so you can switch tasks with a clean working tree.
Reflog
Git's local log of every place HEAD has pointed, used to recover commits after a bad reset or rebase.
Cherry-pick
Copying one specific commit onto the current branch.
Blame
A view showing which commit and author last changed each line of a file.
Amend
Replacing the last commit with a corrected one; only safe before it is pushed.
.gitignore
A file listing paths Git should never track, such as .env, .venv/ and data/.
Personal access token
A generated password with limited scopes and an expiry, used for Git over HTTPS.
Fork
Your own server-side copy of someone else's repository, used to open pull requests without push rights.
Tag
A permanent name, such as v1.4.2, attached to one commit to mark a release.
add_practice: Create a repo with a branch that is 3 commits behind main. Bring it up to date once with git merge and once (after resetting) with git rebase, and compare git log --oneline --graph for both.
Make two commits, run git reset --hard HEAD~2, then recover both commits using only git reflog. Deliverable: the reflog lines you used.
Commit a fake .env file, then stop tracking it with .gitignore and git rm --cached. Install pre-commit with gitleaks and show that a commit containing a fake AWS key is blocked.
Cherry-pick one commit from main onto a release/1.0 branch with -x, then tag the result v1.0.1 and list the tags.

add_subtopics.title: Testing errors, time, files and environment
add_subtopics.body:
Real code does more than return numbers. It raises errors, reads the clock, writes files and reads environment variables. pytest has a built-in tool for each.

pytest.raises checks that code raises an error. Wrap the call in with pytest.raises(ValueError): and the test passes only if that error is raised. Add match= with a piece of the expected message, so a different ValueError from somewhere else does not pass by accident.

pytest.approx compares decimal numbers with a small tolerance. Floats cannot store most decimals exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False in Python. approx makes it pass. For real money, use Decimal in the code; approx is for measurements, averages and ratios.

monkeypatch is a fixture that changes something only for one test and puts it back afterwards. monkeypatch.setenv sets an environment variable, delenv removes one, and setattr swaps an attribute or function.

tmp_path is a fixture that gives each test its own new empty folder, as a pathlib.Path. Write files there, never in the project or your home folder.

Code that calls datetime.now() gives a different answer every day, so its tests break at midnight or on the 1st of the month. Two fixes: pass the current time in as a parameter (an injected clock), or freeze time in the test with the freezegun library, so datetime.now() always returns the moment you choose.
add_subtopics.example: At a housing association you build an arrears checker. Tests prove that a rent split with 0 tenants raises ValueError mentioning 'at least 1', that three-way splits come out at 33.33 within a cent, that the sandbox CRM URL is used when CRM_BASE_URL is set, that the CSV report lands in a temporary folder with the right lines, and that a payment due on 1 March is not overdue on 28 February. All six tests run in 0.1 seconds on any day of the year.
add_subtopics.code:
# app.py
import os, csv
from datetime import datetime, timezone

def split_bill(total: float, people: int) -> float:
    if people <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"people must be at least 1, got {people}")
    return total / people

def api_base_url() -> str:
    return os.environ.get("CRM_BASE_URL", "https://api.crm-example.com")

def write_report(rows, folder) -> str:
    path = folder / "report.csv"
    with open(path, "w", newline="") as f:
        csv.writer(f).writerows(rows)
    return str(path)

def is_overdue(due: datetime, now=None) -> bool:
    now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)   # injectable clock
    return now > due


# test_app.py
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import pytest
from freezegun import freeze_time
from app import split_bill, api_base_url, write_report, is_overdue

def test_split_rejects_zero_people():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="at least 1"):
        split_bill(100.0, 0)

def test_split_three_ways():
    assert split_bill(100.0, 3) == pytest.approx(33.33, abs=0.01)
    assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3)      # plain == would fail

def test_base_url_from_env(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("CRM_BASE_URL", "https://sandbox.crm-example.com")
    assert api_base_url() == "https://sandbox.crm-example.com"
    # monkeypatch undoes the change after the test

def test_report_written(tmp_path):              # a fresh empty folder per test
    path = write_report([["id", "total"], [1, 9.5]], tmp_path)
    assert open(path).read() == "id,total\n1,9.5\n"

DUE = datetime(2026, 3, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)

def test_overdue_with_injected_clock():
    assert is_overdue(DUE, now=datetime(2026, 3, 2, tzinfo=timezone.utc))

@freeze_time("2026-02-28 12:00:00")
def test_not_overdue_with_frozen_clock():
    assert not is_overdue(DUE)

# $ pytest -q
# ......                                   [100%]
# 6 passed

add_subtopics.title: Integration tests against a real database
add_subtopics.body:
Mocks cannot catch a wrong column name or a broken SQL query. For that you need an integration test against a real database of the same kind and version as production, never the customer's live one.

There are two common ways to get a throwaway database. The first is a docker compose file with a postgres service that you start before the tests, locally and in CI. The second is the testcontainers library, which starts a PostgreSQL container from inside a pytest fixture and removes it when the run ends, so nothing needs to be running beforehand. Both need Docker.

The pg_conn fixture used earlier in this lesson is built in two layers. A session-scoped fixture runs once per test run: it connects and creates the tables. A function-scoped fixture runs for every test: it opens a connection, whose work stays inside one open transaction, inserts a few seed rows the test can rely on, hands the connection to the test and rolls everything back afterwards. Every test starts from the same known state, and tests cannot leak rows into each other.

For HTTP APIs, the middle ground between a mock and the real service is a recorded response. The responses library (for requests) and respx (for httpx) let you register a URL and the JSON it should return, and they fail the test if your code calls a URL you did not register. vcrpy goes one step further: it records real replies once into a file (a cassette) and replays them on later runs. Remove tokens and personal data from cassettes before you commit them.
add_subtopics.example: For an insurer's claims loader, the unit tests mocked the database, yet the first deploy failed because the real table called the column policy_no, not policy. After that you add integration tests with the fixtures below. They run against PostgreSQL 16, the same version the insurer uses, and the column-name bug would have failed in CI in 0.2 seconds.

# conftest.py
import os
import psycopg
import pytest

DB_URL = os.environ.get("TEST_DATABASE_URL",
                        "postgresql://postgres@localhost:5433/postgres")

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def pg_setup():
    """Runs once per test run: connect and create the schema."""
    conn = psycopg.connect(DB_URL, autocommit=True)
    conn.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS claims")
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE claims (id serial PRIMARY KEY, policy text NOT NULL,"
                 " amount numeric(10,2) NOT NULL)")
    yield conn                      # tests run here
    conn.execute("DROP TABLE claims")   # teardown after the last test
    conn.close()

@pytest.fixture
def pg_conn(pg_setup):
    """Runs per test: a transaction that is rolled back, so tests never see each other's rows."""
    conn = psycopg.connect(DB_URL)          # autocommit off: everything is one transaction
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO claims (policy, amount) VALUES ('SEED1', 10.00)")  # seed row
    yield conn
    conn.rollback()                         # undo inserts, seeds and all
    conn.close()


# test_loader.py
import pytest
import responses
from loader import load_claims, fetch_policy

@pytest.mark.integration
def test_load_claims_writes_rows(pg_conn):
    load_claims(pg_conn, [{"policy": "ab12", "amount": 50}])
    rows = pg_conn.execute("SELECT policy, amount FROM claims ORDER BY id").fetchall()
    assert [r[0] for r in rows] == ["SEED1", "AB12"]

@pytest.mark.integration
def test_each_test_starts_clean(pg_conn):
    n = pg_conn.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM claims").fetchone()[0]
    assert n == 1                    # only the seed row: the last test was rolled back

@responses.activate
def test_fetch_policy_with_recorded_reply():
    responses.get("https://api.insurer-example.com/v1/policies/P-9",
                  json={"id": "P-9", "status": "active"}, status=200)
    assert fetch_policy("P-9")["status"] == "active"
    assert len(responses.calls) == 1

# $ pytest -q
# ...                                      [100%]
# 3 passed

# conftest.py variant: start a throwaway PostgreSQL in Docker for the test run
import psycopg, pytest
from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def pg_url():
    with PostgresContainer("postgres:16", driver=None) as pg:   # starts, then stops at the end
        yield pg.get_connection_url()

replace_subtopics.title: Your first pytest test
replace_subtopics.body:
In pytest, a test is a plain function whose name starts with test_, in a file whose name starts with test_. Inside it, you call your code and use Python's assert statement to check the result. If the assertion is true, the test passes. If it is false or the code raises an error, the test fails and pytest shows you the values involved.

You run all tests with the command pytest from the project folder. It finds the test files automatically, runs every test function, and prints a summary such as '5 passed, 1 failed'.

Good tests check one behaviour each and have names that read like a sentence. When one fails, the name alone should tell you what broke.

A few command-line flags make pytest much nicer to work with. -x stops at the first failure, so you fix one thing at a time. -k runs only tests whose names match an expression, such as -k discount or -k "member and not under". -vv prints each test name and shows full, untruncated differences when an assertion fails. --lf (last failed) reruns only the tests that failed in the previous run, which is fast when you are fixing a bug. -s shows print() output, which pytest normally hides for passing tests. You can run a single test with its path and name, as in pytest test_pricing.py::test_non_member_pays_full_price.
replace_subtopics.example: A retailer applies a 10% loyalty discount on orders over 100 pounds. You write a function apply_discount(total, is_member). Tests check three facts: a member spending 150 pays 135, a member spending 80 pays 80, and a non-member spending 150 pays 150. Running pytest prints '3 passed'. While fixing the discount rule you run pytest -x -k member to work on member cases only, then pytest --lf to rerun just the two that failed, and finally a plain pytest before you commit.
replace_subtopics.code:
# pricing.py
def apply_discount(total: float, is_member: bool) -> float:
    if is_member and total > 100:
        return round(total * 0.9, 2)
    return total

# test_pricing.py
from pricing import apply_discount

def test_member_over_100_gets_10_percent_off():
    assert apply_discount(150.0, True) == 135.0

def test_member_under_100_pays_full_price():
    assert apply_discount(80.0, True) == 80.0

def test_non_member_pays_full_price():
    assert apply_discount(150.0, False) == 150.0

# $ pytest -q
# ...                                  [100%]
# 3 passed

# $ pytest -x                  # stop at the first failure
# $ pytest -k member           # only tests with 'member' in the name
# 2 passed, 1 deselected
# $ pytest -vv                 # each test name, full assertion diffs
# $ pytest --lf                # rerun only the last failures
# $ pytest -s                  # show print() output
# $ pytest test_pricing.py::test_non_member_pays_full_price   # one test

replace_subtopics.title: Fixtures and parametrised tests
replace_subtopics.body:
A fixture is a function that prepares something a test needs, such as sample data, a temporary file or a database connection. You mark it with @pytest.fixture and name it as a test argument. pytest runs the fixture and passes the result in. Fixtures in a file called conftest.py are shared by all tests in that folder.

Parametrisation runs one test function with many inputs. @pytest.mark.parametrize takes a list of cases and pytest reports each as its own test. This is ideal for data-cleaning rules, where you want to check dozens of messy input values.

Both features keep tests short, which makes them easier to read and more likely to be kept up to date.

A fixture has a scope that controls how often it runs. The default, function, runs it again for every test, which is safest. module runs it once per test file, and session runs it once for the whole test run, which suits slow setup such as starting a database. Share a wider-scoped fixture only if tests cannot change it, or reset it between tests.

Many fixtures also need to clean up. Write the fixture with yield instead of return. Code before yield is setup, the yielded value goes to the test, and code after yield is teardown, which runs even if the test fails. Use it to close connections, delete files or roll back transactions.
replace_subtopics.example: A logistics customer sends postcodes in every format: ' sw1a 1aa', 'SW1A1AA', 'sw1a-1aa'. You write one parametrised test with six input and expected-output pairs for normalise_postcode(). When the customer reports a new format, you add one line to the list, watch it fail, and fix the function. The postcode tests get a shared lookup table of 30,000 valid postcodes that takes 2 seconds to load. You make that fixture session-scoped so it loads once, not 40 times, and the test run drops from 80 seconds to 3.

replace_subtopics.title: CI: tests on every pull request
replace_subtopics.body:
Continuous integration means every change is automatically built and tested on a clean machine, usually when a pull request is opened or updated. GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Jenkins are common CI systems. You describe the steps in a configuration file in the repo.

A typical Python workflow checks out the code, installs a Python version, installs dependencies, and runs pytest. If any test fails, the pull request shows a red cross. With branch protection turned on, a pull request cannot be merged until the required checks pass.

CI also catches the 'works on my machine' problem, because the clean machine has only what the repo declares. Add linting and type checks to the same workflow once tests are in place.

Coverage tells you which lines of your code the tests actually ran. Install pytest-cov and run pytest --cov=src --cov-report=term-missing to see the percentage per file and the line numbers never executed. --cov-fail-under=80 makes the run fail if coverage drops below 80 percent, which is a useful guard in CI. Be clear about what it proves: an uncovered line has definitely never been tested, but a covered line only ran once. It may have no assertion checking it, so a high percentage does not mean the code is correct.

The workflow above installs with pip. If the project uses uv and a lock file, as the take-home layout does, CI should use the same tool so it installs exactly the locked versions. The astral-sh/setup-uv action installs uv and caches downloaded packages between runs, which cuts minutes from each job. Use the same commands in CI as in your README or Makefile, so a green local run means a green CI run.
replace_subtopics.example: At a manufacturer, a customer engineer opens a pull request that renames a column. Two of your unit tests fail in CI because the loader still uses the old name. The pull request is blocked. The engineer fixes the loader in the same pull request, CI turns green, and the change merges without ever breaking the nightly job. At the manufacturer, coverage showed the loader at 64 percent, with the whole bad-row branch never run. You add two tests for malformed rows, reach 91 percent, and set --cov-fail-under=85. A later pull request that adds an untested export path fails CI until its author adds tests.

# .github/workflows/tests.yml
name: tests
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt pytest
      - run: pytest -q          # a failing test fails the job

# Coverage locally
# $ pytest -q --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing --cov-fail-under=80
# Name     Stmts   Miss  Cover   Missing
# app.py      16      0   100%
# Required test coverage of 80% reached. Total coverage: 100.00%

# .github/workflows/tests.yml using uv and its cache
name: tests
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v6
        with:
          enable-cache: true          # reuse downloaded packages between runs
      - run: uv sync --locked         # exact versions from uv.lock
      - run: uv run pytest -q --cov=src --cov-fail-under=80

add_glossary: pytest.raises
A context manager that makes a test pass only if the code inside raises the given error.
pytest.approx
A helper that compares floats with a small tolerance, so 0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.3.
monkeypatch
A pytest fixture that changes environment variables or attributes for one test and restores them afterwards.
tmp_path
A pytest fixture giving each test its own new, empty temporary folder.
Freezing time
Making datetime.now() return a fixed moment in a test, for example with freezegun.
Fixture scope
How often a fixture runs: once per test (function), per file (module) or per run (session).
Yield fixture
A fixture that yields its value and runs cleanup code after the test finishes.
Coverage
The share of code lines that ran during the tests, measured with pytest-cov.
Testcontainers
A library that starts a real database or service in Docker from inside a test fixture.
Recorded response
A saved or registered HTTP reply, used with responses, respx or vcrpy, so tests do not call the real API.

add_subtopics.title: Bugs that only happen sometimes or only in production
add_subtopics.body:
The hardest bugs are the ones you cannot reproduce on your laptop. The code is the same, so something else must differ. Work through a diff checklist and compare production with your machine one item at a time.

Configuration and environment variables: a missing setting, a different feature flag, a different API base URL. Library versions: run pip freeze in both places and diff the output, because a loose requirement such as pandas>=2 can install a different version in the container. Data: production has rows your sample never had, such as nulls, huge values, emoji or a new country. Timezone and locale: servers usually run in UTC, and date parsing or number formatting can change with the locale. Operating system and CPU: Linux in production against macOS on your laptop, or amd64 against arm64. Permissions: the service account cannot read a file or a table your own login can.

Bugs that happen only sometimes usually come from timing or shared state. A race condition happens when two workers read and update the same thing at the same time and the result depends on who is faster. Ordering bugs appear when code assumes results come back in order, but a database without ORDER BY or a parallel job returns them in any order. Caches serve old values after the source changed, and the bug disappears when the cache expires, which makes it look random.

The best evidence is the exact input that failed. Save the failing payload in production with a request ID, after removing personal data and secrets, then replay it locally. Very often the bug reproduces at once.
add_subtopics.example: A travel company's booking sync fails for about 1 in 200 bookings, only in production. The FDE adds code that saves each failing payload, redacted, under its request ID. Two of the saved payloads have a departure time of 02:30 on the night the clocks went forward, a local time that does not exist. The laptop never saw such data. The repro takes one command and the fix converts to UTC before parsing.

import json, hashlib, pathlib, platform, os, time
from importlib.metadata import version

# 1. Print the facts that often differ; run this in BOTH places and compare
def env_report(packages=("requests", "pandas")):
    print("python  ", platform.python_version(), platform.machine())
    print("tz      ", time.tzname, "TZ env:", os.environ.get("TZ"))
    for p in packages:
        print(f"{p:8}", version(p))
# python   3.11.15 x86_64
# tz       ('UTC', 'UTC') TZ env: None
# requests 2.33.1
# pandas   3.0.6
# Also: pip freeze > prod.txt, then diff prod.txt laptop.txt

# 2. Save a failing payload safely, so it can be replayed on a laptop
SENSITIVE = {"email", "name", "phone", "iban", "token"}

def redact(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        return {k: ("<redacted:" + hashlib.sha256(str(v).encode()).hexdigest()[:8] + ">"
                    if k in SENSITIVE else redact(v)) for k, v in obj.items()}
    if isinstance(obj, list):
        return [redact(x) for x in obj]
    return obj

def save_failing_payload(payload, request_id, folder="failed_payloads"):
    path = pathlib.Path(folder) / f"{request_id}.json"
    path.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    path.write_text(json.dumps(redact(payload), indent=1))
    return path

payload = {"order_id": 88213, "email": "a.khan@example.org", "lines": [{"sku": "B-7", "qty": "2"}]}
print(save_failing_payload(payload, "req-7f3a").read_text())

add_subtopics.title: Debugging a running service or container
add_subtopics.body:
Sometimes the bug only shows up inside the deployed service, in a Docker container or a Kubernetes pod. You can still look inside.

First, run commands in the container. docker exec -it <container> sh, or kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh for Kubernetes, opens a shell there. From it you can check environment variables with env, test DNS and network access to a dependency, and run one-line Python checks with python -c, for example importing a library and printing its version, or calling the API the service uses.

Second, raise the log level. Many services read LOG_LEVEL from an environment variable at startup. Set it to DEBUG, restart one instance, reproduce the bug and set it back, because debug logs are large and can contain data you should not keep. Some services also offer an admin endpoint that changes the level without a restart.

Third, attach a real debugger. debugpy is the debug engine behind VS Code's Python debugger. Start the service with python -m debugpy --listen 0.0.0.0:5678 so it waits for a debugger connection. Then forward that port to your laptop with kubectl port-forward pod/<name> 5678:5678 (or publish it with docker run -p 5678:5678), and in VS Code use an Attach configuration pointing at localhost:5678. You can now set breakpoints in the live process. Only do this in a development or staging environment: a paused breakpoint stops that instance from serving anyone.

Finally, follow one request across services by its request ID. If every service logs the same ID, one search in the log tool shows the whole path. The observability topic covers how to set that up.
add_subtopics.example: A document service works locally but returns 500 for PDF uploads in the customer's staging cluster. kubectl exec and python -c show that the image has an older version of the PDF library than the lock file says. To be sure that is the cause, the FDE starts one pod with debugpy, port-forwards 5678, attaches VS Code, and stops at the exact line where the library raises. The image build is fixed to install from the lock file.

replace_subtopics.title: A method: reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, verify
replace_subtopics.body:
Beginners often read the code, guess, change something and rerun, again and again. That works for tiny bugs and wastes hours on real ones. A method is faster.

Reproduce: make the bug happen on demand, ideally on your machine, with the same input, version and settings. If you cannot reproduce it, collect more evidence first (logs, the exact input, the time it happened). Isolate: shrink the problem. Which input, which function, which commit? Hypothesise: write down one specific, testable guess, such as "the total is wrong because amounts with a comma are skipped". Test it: add a print or log, or pause in a debugger, and check. If the guess is wrong, cross it out and make a new one; that is progress too. Fix and verify: change the cause, rerun the original repro, and add a test so the bug cannot quietly return.

Keep a short bug log as you go. It stops you repeating experiments, and it becomes your write-up later.

Set a timebox before you start, for example two hours. When it runs out without progress, stop and escalate: share your bug log with a teammate or the owning team. The log shows what you already ruled out, so they start from where you are, not from zero. Asking early is a skill, not a failure, and customers care more about the fix than about who found it.

When stuck, explain the problem out loud, line by line, to someone else, even a rubber duck on your desk. Saying what each line should do often reveals the line that does not. A coding agent is a good listener too: paste the bug log, the traceback and the relevant function, and ask it to list possible causes and a test for each. Treat its answers as hypotheses to check, never as the fix itself.

Be careful with quick fixes such as removing commas from numbers. They depend on the number format. Many European systems write one thousand two hundred and fifty as 1.250,00, where the dot separates thousands and the comma marks the decimals. Removing commas turns that into 1.25, which is silently wrong. Ask which format each source uses, parse with that format on purpose, and add a test for it.
replace_subtopics.example: A freight company's weekly invoice total is 1,250.00 lower than their ledger. The FDE reproduces it with one week's data, notices the gap equals exactly one invoice, and guesses that invoice is skipped. Logging each parsed total confirms the invoice with "1,250.00" never gets parsed. The fix strips the comma, and a unit test with that exact value is added. At the freight company, a second customer site in Germany sends totals like 1.250,00. The comma fix would have turned them into 1.25 without any error. The FDE asks for the format of each feed, adds a decimal_sep setting per source and a test for both formats, before the German feed is switched on.
replace_subtopics.code:
BUG LOG: invoice total wrong for Tamsel Freight (made up)

Symptom      Weekly total 2,340.10, customer's ledger says 3,590.10
Repro        python sync.py --week 2026-W11   (fails every time on my laptop)
Facts        Diff is exactly 1,250.00. One invoice in that week is 1,250.00.
Hypothesis 1 That invoice is skipped because its total has a comma.
Test         Log each parsed total for W11            -> RESULT: confirmed
Fix          Strip thousands separators before float()
Verify       W11 total now 3,590.10; new unit test passes; W10 unchanged

from decimal import Decimal

def parse_amount(text: str, decimal_sep: str = ".") -> Decimal:
    """Parse '1,250.00' (decimal_sep='.') or '1.250,00' (decimal_sep=',')."""
    thousands_sep = "," if decimal_sep == "." else "."
    cleaned = text.strip().replace(" ", "").replace(thousands_sep, "")
    return Decimal(cleaned.replace(decimal_sep, "."))

print(float("1,250.00".replace(",", "")))        # 1250.0   the quick fix works here
print(float("1.250,00".replace(",", "")))        # 1.25     silently WRONG for a German invoice
print(parse_amount("1,250.00"))                  # 1250.00
print(parse_amount("1.250,00", decimal_sep=",")) # 1250.00
print(parse_amount("1 250,00", decimal_sep=",")) # 1250.00  (French style, space for thousands)

def test_parse_amount_formats():
    assert parse_amount("1,250.00") == Decimal("1250.00")
    assert parse_amount("1.250,00", decimal_sep=",") == Decimal("1250.00")

replace_subtopics.title: Reading tracebacks and logs
replace_subtopics.body:
When Python crashes it prints a traceback: the chain of function calls that were running, oldest at the top and the one that failed at the bottom. Read it from the bottom up. The last line gives the exception type (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError) and a message that often includes the bad value. The frame just above shows the file, line number and code where it broke. Then walk up until you reach the first frame in code you or the customer wrote; frames inside libraries are usually where the error surfaced, not where the mistake was made.

If you see "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred", there are two tracebacks. The first one is usually the real cause.

Logs work the same way. In a noisy log, search for the first ERROR or Traceback around the time of the failure, not the last one, because later errors are often consequences. If requests carry an ID (an order number, a request ID), grep for that ID to follow one request through many services.

You also write the code that produces tracebacks, so make them useful to the next person. Inside an except block, log with log.exception("message"). It logs at ERROR level and adds the full traceback. log.error("message", exc_info=True) does the same. A plain log.error(str(e)) keeps only the message and throws away the file and line numbers you need later.

When you catch a low-level error and raise a clearer one, write raise NewError("what failed and for which record") from e. The word from links the two, and the traceback shows both with the line "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception". Without from, Python shows "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred", which suggests a second bug. Never catch an error and carry on without logging it, because that is how data disappears silently.
replace_subtopics.example: A claims integration crashes overnight and the log shows 300 errors. The FDE runs grep for ERROR and looks at the first hit: a single ValueError about a date "31/02/2026" at 01:12. Every later error is "record not found", caused by the first failure stopping the batch. Fixing date validation removes all 300. The invoice loader now skips a bad row instead of crashing the whole batch. Because it uses log.exception and raise ... from e, the log line says which invoice failed, shows the original ValueError with its bad value, and points at the exact line. The on-call engineer at the customer can fix the source data without calling you.

Traceback (most recent call last):          <- read from the BOTTOM up
  File "invoices.py", line 10, in <module>   <- outermost call (where it started)
    print(load(payload))
  File "invoices.py", line 8, in load
    return sum(parse_total(r) for r in rows)
  File "invoices.py", line 8, in <genexpr>
    return sum(parse_total(r) for r in rows)
  File "invoices.py", line 4, in parse_total  <- last frame: where it broke
    return float(line["total"])
ValueError: could not convert string to float: '1,250.00'
^ exception type    ^ message, often with the bad value

$ grep -n -E "ERROR|Traceback" app.log | head -3
$ grep -n "order 88213" app.log            # follow one request by its id

import logging
log = logging.getLogger("invoices")

class InvoiceParseError(Exception):
    pass

def parse_total(row):
    try:
        return float(row["total"])
    except ValueError as e:
        # "from e" keeps the original error attached as the cause
        raise InvoiceParseError(f"invoice {row['id']}: bad total {row['total']!r}") from e

def load(rows):
    good = []
    for row in rows:
        try:
            good.append(parse_total(row))
        except InvoiceParseError:
            log.exception("skipping row")   # ERROR level WITH the full traceback
            # same as: log.error("skipping row", exc_info=True)
    return sum(good)

# ERROR invoices: skipping row
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "invoices.py", line 9, in parse_total
#     return float(row["total"])

add_glossary: Race condition
A bug where the result depends on which of two concurrent operations finishes first.
Environment diff
Comparing config, library versions, data, timezone, OS and permissions between where a bug happens and where it does not.
Replay
Running saved real input, with personal data removed, through the code locally to reproduce a bug.
debugpy
The Python debug engine behind VS Code, which can attach to a running process over a network port.
Port-forward
A kubectl command that connects a port on your laptop to a port inside a pod.
log.exception
A logging call used inside except that records the message at ERROR level plus the full traceback.
Exception chaining
raise NewError(...) from e, which keeps the original error attached as the cause.
Timebox
A fixed amount of time you allow for an investigation before you escalate.
Rubber-duck debugging
Explaining the code line by line to someone or something else until the mistake becomes obvious.

add_subtopics.title: Driving an agent session: plan first, permissions and context
add_subtopics.body:
How you run a session matters as much as what you ask.

Plan first. For anything bigger than a small fix, ask the agent for a plan before it edits a file: which files it will change, in what order, and how it will test. Claude Code has a plan mode for this (Shift+Tab cycles the modes), and other tools have similar ask or plan modes. Correcting a plan takes a minute; undoing a wrong 30-file change takes an hour.

Set permissions on purpose. Agents ask before running commands or editing files, and a settings file lets you decide in advance. In Claude Code, .claude/settings.json has allow and deny lists: allow safe, frequent commands such as running tests, and deny reading .env files or running deploy commands. Commit the project settings so the whole team shares them.

Manage the context window. The model can only hold a limited amount of text at once, and a long session fills it with old files, logs and dead ends. Start a fresh session for each new task, use /clear between unrelated tasks, and put lasting knowledge in CLAUDE.md, not in chat history. When a long session is compacted (summarised to free space), details can drift, so restate the key rules or start over.

Run agents in parallel safely. git worktree add creates a second working folder of the same repository on another branch. Each agent gets its own worktree and branch, so they never edit the same files at once.

Use agents headless. claude -p runs one prompt without the interactive screen, which suits scripts and CI jobs, such as a first-pass review of every pull request. Give headless runs the smallest set of allowed tools.
add_subtopics.example: At a utilities customer, an FDE must add a new meter type to three services. She asks for a plan, spots that the agent wants to edit a generated file, and corrects it. She then opens two worktrees, one per service, and runs one agent in each with the shared settings file that allows pytest and ruff but denies .env and kubectl. A CI job runs claude -p on each pull request to list risky changes for the human reviewer.

// .claude/settings.json (committed, shared by the team)
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(pytest:*)", "Bash(ruff check:*)", "Bash(git diff:*)"],
    "deny":  ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./secrets/**)", "Bash(kubectl:*)", "Bash(curl:*)"]
  }
}

# Parallel agents, one worktree and branch each
git worktree add ../meters-api -b feat/meter-type-api
git worktree add ../meters-etl -b feat/meter-type-etl
git worktree list
# (run one agent session inside each folder; remove with: git worktree remove ../meters-api)

# Headless, for scripts and CI: one prompt, limited tools, output to a file
claude -p "Review the diff against main. List risky changes: auth, deletes, new dependencies." \
  --allowedTools "Bash(git diff:*)" "Read" > review.md

# Inside a session
# Shift+Tab   cycle modes, including plan mode (no edits until you approve)
# /clear      start fresh before an unrelated task

replace_subtopics.title: Security and data rules on customer systems
replace_subtopics.body:
At a customer, their rules decide which tools you may use and what they may see. Before using any AI tool on their code, ask which tools are approved, under which accounts, and with which settings. Many companies allow only enterprise plans with agreed data handling, or only tools running against models inside their own cloud.

Keep sensitive data out of prompts. That includes credentials, API keys, connection strings, personal data about their customers or staff, and anything marked confidential. Use synthetic or masked data for tests and examples. Remember that an agent reading files can pick up a .env file or a data export in the folder, so keep those out of the working directory or excluded.

Limit what the agent can do. Give it the least access it needs: a development environment, read-only database users, no production credentials. Review or approve shell commands rather than allowing everything, especially anything that deletes, deploys or sends data out. Agents can also be steered by instructions hidden in files or web pages they read (prompt injection), so do not let an agent with broad permissions process untrusted content unattended.

Watch every new dependency an agent adds. Models sometimes suggest a package name that sounds right but does not exist. Attackers register such invented names on PyPI and npm with malicious code, which is called slopsquatting; typo-squatting is the same trick with misspellings such as reqeusts. Before installing, check that the package exists, is the one you meant, has a real project page and history, and pin the exact version in the lock file. Better still, ask the agent to use the standard library or a dependency the project already has.

Finally, read the contract. Many statements of work (SOWs) and master agreements now say who owns AI-generated code, whether AI tools may be used at all, and whether generated code must be scanned for licensed open source snippets. Some customers also require you to record which changes were AI-assisted, for example with a commit trailer. Check with your account lead before the first commit, not after.
replace_subtopics.example: At Fenwick Mutual, an insurer, the security team approved one coding tool on an enterprise plan, for the development environment only. The FDE kept claim exports outside the repository, created a masked sample of 50 claims for tests, used a read-only database user, and set the agent to ask before running any command. When an auditor asked months later how AI tools had been used, she could answer with the approval email and the settings file. On the same project an agent suggested pip install dateutil-parser-pro. A quick PyPI check showed the package did not exist, so the FDE used python-dateutil, already approved, instead. Fenwick's contract also required a trailer on AI-assisted commits, so the team added Assisted-by lines.

import requests

def check_package(name: str) -> str:
    """Look a package up on PyPI before installing something an agent suggested."""
    r = requests.get(f"https://pypi.org/pypi/{name}/json", timeout=10)
    if r.status_code == 404:
        return f"{name}: NOT ON PyPI, possibly invented; do not install"
    data = r.json()
    uploads = [f["upload_time"][:10] for files in data["releases"].values() for f in files]
    return f"{name}: latest {data['info']['version']}, first upload {min(uploads)}"

for name in ["python-dateutil", "dateutil-parser-pro"]:
    print(check_package(name))
# python-dateutil: latest 2.9.0.post0, first upload 2008-08-06
# dateutil-parser-pro: NOT ON PyPI, possibly invented; do not install

# Record AI assistance when the customer's policy asks for it
# git commit -m "Parse policy dates in UTC" -m "Assisted-by: coding agent (approved enterprise plan)"
