replace_subtopics.title: Giving context: CLAUDE.md, specs, tests
replace_subtopics.body:
An agent only knows what it can read. Three kinds of context make the biggest difference.

A project rules file is a short file in the repository that the tool reads at the start of every session. Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md; Cursor and Copilot have their own equivalents. Put in it how to build and test, the folder layout, coding conventions, and hard rules such as 'never edit generated files' or 'all database access goes through repo/'. Keep it short and correct; stale rules mislead.

A spec is a few lines on what to build: inputs, outputs, edge cases and what done means. Writing it forces you to think, and the agent follows it far better than a one-line request.

Tests first means you write, or ask the agent to write, failing tests that describe the behaviour before the implementation. The tests become an objective check, and you can see if the agent later tries to change them to pass.

Context does not have to be files in the repository. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets an agent connect to other systems through small servers: the customer's ticket tracker, their internal docs, or a database. With the ticket server the agent can read the actual ticket instead of your summary, and with a database server it can check the real schema before writing a query. Use only servers the customer approves, and give each the narrowest access: a read-only database user on a development copy, read access to one project in the tracker. Anything the agent reads through MCP is also untrusted content, so the prompt injection rules in the security section apply. The MCP topic explains how servers work.
replace_subtopics.example: An FDE at Lanternfield Clinics needed a function to normalise appointment times from three source systems. He wrote a six-line spec, listed five edge cases (missing timezone, daylight saving change, 24:00, blank, two formats in one file), asked the agent to write failing tests for those first, reviewed the tests, then asked for the implementation. The first version failed two tests; the second passed all of them. At Lanternfield Clinics, the FDE connected the agent to the ticket tracker with a read-only token for one project. The agent read the ticket, including a comment from a nurse listing a sixth edge case the FDE had missed, and added a test for it.

# CLAUDE.md  (project rules file, read at the start of each session)

## Build and test
- Install: pip install -e .[dev]
- Run tests: pytest -q   (must pass before any commit)
- Lint: ruff check .

## Layout
- src/connectors/  one module per customer system (read-only clients)
- src/pipeline/    transforms; pure functions, no network calls
- tests/           mirrors src/; fixtures in tests/fixtures (synthetic data only)

## Rules
- Never edit files in src/generated/ (built from the OpenAPI spec).
- No real customer data in tests or prompts. Use tests/fixtures.
- Do not change an existing test to make it pass; ask first.
- Keep changes small: one feature or fix per commit.

claude mcp add --transport http tickets https://mcp.tickets-example.com/mcp
claude mcp list

add_subtopics.title: Measure before you optimise: profiling Python
add_subtopics.body:
When a customer says "the job is slow", do not guess which line is to blame. Measure first, change one thing, then measure again.

Start with a stopwatch. time.perf_counter() gives a precise clock: read it before and after a step and subtract. This tells you how long the whole job or one stage takes.

For comparing two small pieces of code, use timeit. It runs a statement many times and reports the total, which smooths out noise. It is ideal for questions like "is a set lookup really faster than a list lookup here?"

To find where the time goes in a real program, use a profiler. cProfile ships with Python. It counts every function call and how long each took. Sort by tottime (time spent inside the function itself) to find the hot spot. snakeviz draws the same data as a clickable chart. py-spy is a separate tool that can attach to a program that is already running, even in production, without changing its code, and can draw a flame graph: a picture where the widest bars are the functions using the most time.

Memory is the other half. tracemalloc, also built in, reports how much memory Python allocated and the peak. Use it when a job dies with MemoryError or the container is killed for using too much RAM.

Once you know the hot spot, the fix is often one of the Big-O fixes in this lesson: a set instead of a list, one bulk query instead of many, or streaming instead of loading everything.
add_subtopics.example: A retail customer's nightly SKU matching job grows from 10 minutes to 3 hours. replace_subtopics.title: What Big-O measures
replace_subtopics.body:
Big-O counts how the number of basic steps grows with input size, written n. It ignores constant factors and small terms, because at large n the biggest term dominates. A function doing 3n + 50 steps is O(n). One doing n^2 + 1000n is O(n^2).

The common classes, from fastest to slowest growth, are: O(1), constant, the same work whatever n is. O(log n), logarithmic, where each step halves what remains. O(n), linear, touching each item once. O(n log n), typical of efficient sorting. O(n^2), quadratic, usually a loop inside a loop.

The gaps get huge fast. For n = 1,000,000: log n is about 20, n log n is about 20 million, and n^2 is a trillion.

Best, average and worst case. The same code can take different amounts of work depending on the data. Searching a list for a value is best case O(1) when it is the first item, average case about n/2 steps (still O(n)), and worst case n steps when it is last or missing. When people give one Big-O for an algorithm, they usually mean the worst case, except for hash tables. A dict lookup is O(1) on average but can be O(n) in a rare worst case when many keys land in the same slot. That is what "O(1) on average" means elsewhere in this lesson.

Amortised O(1). list.append is described as O(1) even though, now and then, the list is full and Python must allocate a bigger block and copy every item. Because the block grows by a proportion each time, those copies are rare, and averaged over many appends the cost per append stays constant. That average over a long sequence of operations is called amortised cost. Dicts grow the same way.

Space complexity in practice. Memory grows with n too. Loading a whole file into a list is O(n) memory; reading it one row at a time with a generator, or in chunks with pandas read_csv(chunksize=...), is O(1) memory for the rows, because only a small running total is kept. A 10 GB file will not fit in an 8 GB container, but it can be streamed.
replace_subtopics.example: A bank has 1 million transactions. Checking whether one account id is in a Python set takes about one step. Binary search on a sorted list takes about 20 comparisons. Scanning a list takes up to 1 million. Comparing every transaction with every other to find duplicates takes about 500 billion comparisons, which at roughly 10 million comparisons per second in plain Python is over 13 hours. At a utilities customer, an FDE must total 10 GB of meter readings on a small container. Loading the file with pandas crashes; reading it in 50,000-row chunks and adding each chunk's totals finishes in minutes using a few hundred MB.

replace_subtopics.title: List versus dict: the most common fix
replace_subtopics.body:
In Python, checking x in some_list walks the list from the start until it finds x, so it is O(n). Checking x in some_set or x in some_dict uses a hash table: Python computes a number from x and jumps straight to the right slot, so it is O(1) on average.

The trap appears when the list check sits inside a loop. For each of n orders, you scan m customers. That is O(n times m). With 50,000 of each, it is up to 2.5 billion comparisons.

The fix is to build a dict or set once, in O(m), and then look each item up in O(1). Total work becomes O(n + m). You trade some memory for the index, which is almost always worth it.

A few other everyday operations hide an O(n) loop inside one innocent-looking call:

list.pop(0) and list.insert(0, x) shift every other item by one place, so using a list as a queue is O(n) per step. Use collections.deque, whose popleft() and appendleft() are O(1).

Building a long string or bytes value with += in a loop can copy everything built so far on each step, which is O(n^2) in total. CPython sometimes optimises the str case, but you cannot rely on it, and bytes always pays. Collect the pieces in a list and call "".join(pieces) once.

x in some_dict.values() is a linear scan, because values are not indexed, only keys are. If you need to look up by value often, build a reverse dict once.
replace_subtopics.example: An e-commerce FDE matches 200,000 payments to 200,000 invoices by invoice number. The first version loops over payments and, for each, searches the invoice list. It is still running after an hour. Building invoices_by_number = {inv['number']: inv for inv in invoices} and looking each payment up takes under a second. A logistics FDE finds a retry queue built with list.pop(0) taking most of a job's time once it holds 100,000 items; switching to deque removes it from the profile entirely.

invoices = [{"number": f"INV-{i}", "amount": i % 500} for i in range(200_000)]
payments = [{"ref": f"INV-{i}", "paid": i % 500} for i in range(0, 400_000, 2)]

# Slow: O(n * m). 'in' on a list scans it every time.
# numbers = [inv["number"] for inv in invoices]
# matched = [p for p in payments if p["ref"] in numbers]

# Fast: O(n + m). Build the index once.
by_number = {inv["number"]: inv for inv in invoices}     # O(m)
matched, unmatched = [], []
for p in payments:                                       # O(n)
    inv = by_number.get(p["ref"])                        # O(1) average
    (matched if inv else unmatched).append(p)

print(len(matched), "matched,", len(unmatched), "unmatched")

import time
from collections import deque

def timed(label, fn):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    fn()
    print(f"{label:28} {time.perf_counter() - t:6.3f} s")

N = 100_000

def queue_list():
    q = list(range(N))
    while q:
        q.pop(0)            # O(n): every other item shifts left

def queue_deque():
    q = deque(range(N))
    while q:
        q.popleft()         # O(1): built for both ends

def build_plus():
    b = b""
    for i in range(N):
        b += b"%d," % i     # copies everything built so far, every time

def build_join():
    b = b",".join(b"%d" % i for i in range(N))   # one pass, one copy

prices = {f"SKU-{i}": i for i in range(N)}
def search_values():
    return sum(1 for p in range(N - 2_000, N) if p in prices.values())  # O(n) each

reverse = {v: k for k, v in prices.items()}   # build once, O(n)
def search_reverse():
    return sum(1 for p in range(N - 2_000, N) if p in reverse)          # O(1) each

timed("list.pop(0) queue", queue_list)
timed("deque.popleft() queue", queue_deque)
timed("bytes += in a loop", build_plus)
timed("bytes join", build_join)
timed("x in dict.values() x2000", search_values)
timed("x in reverse dict x2000", search_reverse)

replace_subtopics.title: Hidden loops: N+1 queries and API calls
replace_subtopics.body:
Complexity is not only about loops you can see. Calling a database or an API inside a loop multiplies slow network round trips by n. This is called the N+1 problem: one query to get a list, then one more query per item.

A network call might take 20 to 200 milliseconds, while a dict lookup takes well under a microsecond. So 10,000 calls in a loop can take many minutes even though the Big-O looks like a harmless O(n).

The fix is to fetch in bulk. Use a single SQL query with a JOIN or WHERE id IN (...), or an API's batch endpoint, then build a dict in memory and look up from it.

pandas has its own version of this trap. df.iterrows() and df.apply(..., axis=1) run a Python function once per row, which is hundreds of times slower than a vectorised operation that works on a whole column at once, such as df["qty"] * df["price"]. Worse is a lookup inside apply, such as filtering the customers table once per order: that is O(n times m), a hidden nested loop. Replace it with one merge, which builds a hash index like a dict and is O(n + m). The table shows timings from one run on 200,000 orders and 5,000 customers; the pandas topic covers vectorised operations and merge in more detail.
replace_subtopics.example: A healthcare dashboard loads 3,000 appointments, then queries the patients table once per appointment to get the name. At 30 ms per query that is 90 seconds per page load. Rewriting it as one query that joins appointments to patients returns everything in about 200 ms. At a retailer, an order report used apply to look up each order's region in a customers DataFrame. On 2,000 rows it took half a second; on the full 200,000 it would take about a minute. One merge did all 200,000 rows in a twentieth of a second.

add_subtopics.title: Rate limiting yourself and circuit breakers
add_subtopics.body:
Backoff reacts after the API complains. It is better not to trip the limit in the first place, and to stop calling an API that is clearly down.

A client-side rate limiter keeps you under the customer's limit. The simplest is a fixed pace, such as one request every 0.2 seconds for 5 per second. A token bucket is more flexible: the bucket holds up to N tokens and refills at a steady rate; each request takes one token and waits if the bucket is empty. It allows a short burst and then settles at the agreed rate. Set it a little below the published limit, because other systems may share the same API key.

A concurrency cap limits how many requests are in flight at once. In async code use asyncio.Semaphore(3); with threads, a worker pool of 3. Rate and concurrency are different: 3 slow requests in flight might only be 1 per second.

A circuit breaker protects both sides when the API is failing. It counts failures in a row. After a threshold, the circuit opens and calls fail immediately without touching the network, for a cool-down period. Then it lets one trial call through (half-open). If that works, the circuit closes and traffic resumes; if not, it opens again. Without it, 20 workers keep hammering a dead server with retries, filling logs and slowing its recovery.

Libraries exist for all three (aiolimiter, pybreaker), but the logic is small enough to read in full below.
add_subtopics.example: A logistics customer's shipment API allows 300 requests per minute per key, shared with their own mobile app. The FDE sets a token bucket at 4 per second (240 per minute) and 3 requests in flight. One night the API goes down for 20 minutes. After 3 failures the breaker opens, the job pauses for 60 seconds at a time instead of firing thousands of retries, and it carries on when the API returns.
add_subtopics.code:
import asyncio, time

class TokenBucket:
    """Allow `rate` calls per second on average, with bursts up to `capacity`."""
    def __init__(self, rate: float, capacity: int):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate, capacity
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.updated = time.monotonic()
        self.lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def acquire(self):
        async with self.lock:
            while True:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self.tokens = min(self.capacity,
                                  self.tokens + (now - self.updated) * self.rate)
                self.updated = now
                if self.tokens >= 1:
                    self.tokens -= 1
                    return
                await asyncio.sleep((1 - self.tokens) / self.rate)  # wait for next token

class CircuitOpen(Exception):
    pass

class CircuitBreaker:
    """After `threshold` failures in a row, refuse calls for `cooldown` seconds."""
    def __init__(self, threshold: int = 5, cooldown: float = 30.0):
        self.threshold, self.cooldown = threshold, cooldown
        self.failures, self.opened_at = 0, None

    async def call(self, fn, *args):
        if self.opened_at is not None:
            if time.monotonic() - self.opened_at < self.cooldown:
                raise CircuitOpen("customer API is down, not calling it")
            self.opened_at = None                 # half-open: allow one trial call
        try:
            result = await fn(*args)
        except Exception:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.failures >= self.threshold:
                self.opened_at = time.monotonic() # open the circuit
            raise
        self.failures = 0                         # success closes it again
        return result

bucket = TokenBucket(rate=5, capacity=5)          # stay under 5 requests/second
limit = asyncio.Semaphore(3)                      # at most 3 requests in flight
breaker = CircuitBreaker(threshold=3, cooldown=2.0)

async def fake_api(page):                          # stands in for session.get(...)
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    if 10 <= page < 16:
        raise ConnectionError("503")               # the API goes down for a while
    return {"page": page}

async def fetch(page):
    await bucket.acquire()
    async with limit:
        return await breaker.call(fake_api, page)

async def main():
    start = time.monotonic()
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(p) for p in range(20)),
                                   return_exceptions=True)
    ok = sum(isinstance(r, dict) for r in results)
    down = sum(isinstance(r, ConnectionError) for r in results)
    skipped = sum(isinstance(r, CircuitOpen) for r in results)
    print(f"{ok} ok, {down} failed calls, {skipped} skipped by the breaker, "
          f"{time.monotonic() - start:.1f} s")

asyncio.run(main())
# 10 ok, 3 failed calls, 7 skipped by the breaker, 3.0 s

replace_subtopics.title: Timeouts and error classes
replace_subtopics.body:
Every HTTP call needs a timeout, which is a maximum time to wait for a reply. Without one, a stuck server can freeze your worker forever.

HTTP status codes tell you what went wrong. Codes 200 to 299 mean success. 429 means 'too many requests', you hit a rate limit. 500 to 599 mean the server had a problem. Most other 4xx codes, like 400, 401, 403, 404 and 422, mean your request is wrong.

This gives a simple rule. Transient errors (429, 5xx, timeouts, connection resets) may succeed later, so retry them. Permanent errors (most 4xx) will fail again, so stop and fix the cause.

One 4xx code deserves special care: 401 Unauthorized. With OAuth, access tokens expire after a set time, often one hour, so a 401 in a long job is often just an expired token, not a bug. The http topic says to refresh the token and retry once, and this lesson says to stop on 401; both are right, in order. Refresh the token once and repeat the request. If the second attempt also returns 401, the credentials themselves are wrong or revoked, so stop and alert a person. Never loop on refresh. A 403 Forbidden means the token is valid but lacks permission, so refreshing will not help.
replace_subtopics.example: A pipeline calls a retailer's orders API. At 09:00 it gets a 503 because the server is restarting. Retrying 4 seconds later works. At 09:05 it gets a 401 because the API token expired. Retrying 50 times would just fill the logs, so the job stops and alerts the FDE to rotate the token. In the same pipeline, the access token expires at 10:00 in the middle of a run. The next call gets a 401, the client refreshes the token once, and the run continues. The 09:05 case above is different: it uses a static API key with nothing to refresh, so stopping and alerting is right. And when a refresh itself returns 401, for example because the customer rotated the client secret, the job also stops and pages the FDE.

replace_subtopics.title: Backoff, jitter and Retry-After
replace_subtopics.body:
Retrying immediately after a failure usually fails again and adds load to a struggling server. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure: 1 second, then 2, then 4, then 8.

Jitter adds a small random amount to each wait. Without it, 20 parallel workers that failed at the same moment all retry at the same moment, and the server gets hit in waves.

Some servers send a Retry-After header saying exactly how long to wait. Honour it when present. Always cap the number of attempts, then fail loudly so a person can look.

Note that the plain tenacity setup above ignores Retry-After: wait_exponential_jitter only knows its own schedule. To honour the header, keep its value on the exception and give tenacity a custom wait function that uses it when present and falls back to backoff otherwise. The header comes in two forms: a number of seconds, such as Retry-After: 120, or an HTTP date, such as Retry-After: Wed, 30 Sep 2026 10:00:30 GMT. Handle both, and cap the wait so a strange value cannot pause the job for a day.
replace_subtopics.example: An FDE runs 10 workers against a CRM API limited to 100 requests per minute. Without jitter, all 10 get 429s together and retry together every few seconds. With exponential backoff plus jitter, retries spread out, and the job finishes its 50,000 records in about 9 minutes without tripping the limit again. On the CRM job, the API starts returning Retry-After: 60 on its 429s. With the custom wait, workers pause the full 60 seconds instead of retrying after 1, 2 and 4 seconds, and the 429s stop.

replace_subtopics.title: Pagination and checkpoints
replace_subtopics.body:
APIs return large results in pages. Offset pagination ('give me rows 1000 to 1500') can skip or repeat rows if data changes during the pull. Cursor pagination returns a token pointing to where the next page starts, which is stable.

A checkpoint is a saved cursor. After each page is stored, write the cursor to a file or table. If the job crashes on page 812, it can resume from page 812 instead of starting over.

For very large backfills, first ask the customer whether a bulk export or a webhook exists. It is often faster than paging through millions of records.

Two details make checkpoints safe. First, the cursor checkpoint is only for resuming one backfill. When the last page arrives, next_cursor is empty; if you save that empty value, the next scheduled run loads None and starts the whole backfill again. Instead, mark the backfill as done and record a watermark, the time the backfill started. Later runs ask only for records changed since the watermark (for example updated_since=...) and move it forward. Start the watermark a little early, since records edited during the backfill must not be missed; upserts make any overlap harmless.

Second, write the checkpoint atomically. If the process dies half way through writing checkpoint.json, the file can be left empty or broken, and the next run fails to read it. Write to a temporary file in the same folder, flush it to disk, then call os.replace, which swaps the new file in as one step: readers see either the old checkpoint or the new one, never half of each. A database table updated in the same transaction as the data is even safer.
replace_subtopics.example: A hospital scheduling API returns 200 appointments per page. The initial backfill is 1.8 million appointments, about 9,000 pages. The job crashes at page 4,120 due to a network outage. Because the cursor was saved after each page, the rerun continues from 4,120 and finishes in half the time. On the next night's run the job sees backfill_done and a watermark, and fetches only the 6,000 appointments updated since then, instead of starting the 9,000 pages again.

import json, os, pathlib, tempfile

CHECKPOINT = pathlib.Path("checkpoint.json")

def load_state():
    if CHECKPOINT.exists():
        return json.loads(CHECKPOINT.read_text())
    return {"cursor": None, "backfill_done": False, "watermark": None}

def save_state(state):
    # Atomic write: write a temp file in the same folder, then swap it in.
    # A crash mid-write leaves the old checkpoint intact, never half a file.
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=CHECKPOINT.parent, suffix=".tmp")
    with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
        json.dump(state, f)
        f.flush()
        os.fsync(f.fileno())
    os.replace(tmp, CHECKPOINT)

def backfill(fetch_page, sink, started_at):
    """Resumable one-off backfill. The cursor is only for resuming THIS run."""
    state = load_state()
    if state["backfill_done"]:
        return state
    while True:
        page = fetch_page(state["cursor"])
        sink.write(page["data"])                      # store first...
        next_cursor = page.get("next_cursor")
        if not next_cursor:                           # last page: do NOT save a null
            state.update(cursor=None, backfill_done=True, watermark=started_at)
            save_state(state)                         # later runs go incremental
            return state
        state["cursor"] = next_cursor
        save_state(state)                             # ...then checkpoint

# Later scheduled runs: ask only for what changed since the watermark, e.g.
# GET /v1/orders?updated_since=<watermark>, then move the watermark forward.

# --- quick check with a fake API of 3 pages ---
class Sink:
    def __init__(self): self.rows = []
    def write(self, rows): self.rows += rows
pages = {None: {"data": [1, 2], "next_cursor": "c2"},
         "c2": {"data": [3, 4], "next_cursor": "c3"},
         "c3": {"data": [5], "next_cursor": None}}
CHECKPOINT.unlink(missing_ok=True)
sink = Sink()
print(backfill(pages.get, sink, "2026-09-29T02:00:00Z"), sink.rows)
print(backfill(pages.get, Sink(), "2026-09-30T02:00:00Z"))   # second run: no restart
# {'cursor': None, 'backfill_done': True, 'watermark': '2026-09-29T02:00:00Z'} [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# {'cursor': None, 'backfill_done': True, 'watermark': '2026-09-29T02:00:00Z'}

replace_subtopics.title: Test the failure paths first
replace_subtopics.body:
Test-Driven Development (TDD) means writing a failing test before the code that makes it pass. For ingestion, the most valuable tests cover failures: a 429, a 500, a timeout and a malformed record.

You do not want to call the real customer API in tests. A mock replaces it with a fake that returns whatever you script. The responses library does this for requests.

Keep changes small and reviewed. Commit each fix on a feature branch with its test, and open a pull request so a teammate can check the retry logic.

One snag: the retry test above really waits, because wait_exponential_jitter sleeps 1 second, then about 2, between attempts, and a Retry-After of 120 would wait two minutes. Tests must stay fast, so replace the wait in tests only. With tenacity, set fetch_page.retry.wait to wait_none() in a fixture; pytest's monkeypatch puts the original back after each test. The retry logic, attempt count and error classes are still exercised; only the sleeping is removed. Test the wait function itself separately, as a plain function.
replace_subtopics.example: Before writing fetch_page, the FDE writes a test where the fake API returns 429, then 503, then 200. The test asserts that the function returns the data and made exactly 3 calls. A second test returns 401 and asserts that the function fails after 1 call. The FDE's suite of 14 retry tests took 40 seconds because every test slept. After adding the fixture it runs in under a second, so people actually run it before each commit.

add_glossary: Token bucket
A rate limiter that holds up to N tokens, refills at a steady rate and spends one per request.
Concurrency cap
A limit on how many requests are in flight at once, for example with asyncio.Semaphore.
Circuit breaker
A guard that stops calling a failing service for a cool-down period after repeated errors.
Half-open
The circuit breaker state that lets one trial call through to see if the service has recovered.
Watermark
A saved timestamp marking how far data has been loaded, used to fetch only newer changes next time.
Atomic write
Writing a file so readers see the old or new version but never a half-written one, for example with os.replace.
Retry-After
An HTTP response header telling the client how long to wait, as seconds or a date, before trying again.
Token refresh
Getting a new OAuth access token with a refresh token or client credentials when the old one expires.

add_subtopics.title: Anti-joins, EXISTS and deduplication with ROW_NUMBER
add_subtopics.body:
Three query shapes come up in almost every engagement and interview.

An anti-join finds rows in A with no match in B: customers with no orders, invoices with no payment. There are two good ways. LEFT JOIN B and keep rows WHERE the B key IS NULL: the left join fills NULL when nothing matched, so those are exactly the unmatched rows. Or write WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE ...), which reads like the question and is the safest form.

Avoid NOT IN with a subquery. If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all, because x NOT IN (1, NULL) means x <> 1 AND x <> NULL, and a comparison with NULL is unknown. Real tables often have NULL foreign keys, so this bug silently returns an empty result.

A semi-join is the opposite: rows in A that have at least one match in B. WHERE EXISTS returns each A row once, however many matches B has, so it never fans out the way a plain JOIN does.

Deduplication keeps one row per key, usually the latest. Number the rows inside each key with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY loaded_at DESC) and keep rn = 1. Add a tie-breaker column to the ORDER BY so the choice is repeatable when two rows share a timestamp. Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and DuckDB offer QUALIFY, which filters on a window function directly and saves the outer query. PostgreSQL also has DISTINCT ON (key) for the same job.
add_subtopics.example: A telecom's CRM export has 2.1 million customer rows but only 1.9 million distinct customer ids, because every edit adds a new row. The FDE keeps the latest row per id with ROW_NUMBER, then uses NOT EXISTS to list 3,400 customers with no billing account. An earlier NOT IN version had returned zero rows, because 12 billing accounts had a NULL customer_id.
add_subtopics.code:
CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id int PRIMARY KEY, name text);
CREATE TABLE orders (order_id int PRIMARY KEY, customer_id int, amount numeric);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Arden Bikes'),(2,'Birchway Cafe'),(3,'Coldharbour Gym'),(4,'Dunmore Books');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,120),(11,1,80),(12,3,45),(13,NULL,60);   -- one NULL customer_id

-- Anti-join 1: LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM   customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE  o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER  BY c.customer_id;
-- 2 | Birchway Cafe
-- 4 | Dunmore Books

-- Anti-join 2: NOT EXISTS (same 2 rows, the safest form)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM   customers c
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER  BY c.customer_id;

-- The trap: NOT IN returns 0 rows because the subquery contains a NULL
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM   customers c
WHERE  c.customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
-- (0 rows)

-- Semi-join: customers with at least one order, each listed once
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM   customers c
WHERE  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER  BY c.customer_id;
-- 1 | Arden Bikes        (2 orders, still 1 row)
-- 3 | Coldharbour Gym

-- Dedupe: keep the latest row per customer
CREATE TABLE customer_updates (customer_id int, email text, loaded_at timestamp);
INSERT INTO customer_updates VALUES
 (1,'old@arden.example','2026-09-01 08:00'),(1,'new@arden.example','2026-09-03 08:00'),
 (2,'hi@birchway.example','2026-09-02 08:00'),(2,'hi@birchway.example','2026-09-02 08:00');

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY loaded_at DESC, email) AS rn   -- email breaks ties
  FROM   customer_updates
)
SELECT customer_id, email, loaded_at
FROM   ranked
WHERE  rn = 1
ORDER  BY customer_id;
-- 1 | new@arden.example   | 2026-09-03 08:00:00
-- 2 | hi@birchway.example | 2026-09-02 08:00:00

-- Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, DuckDB: QUALIFY does it without the CTE
-- SELECT customer_id, email, loaded_at
-- FROM   customer_updates
-- QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY loaded_at DESC, email) = 1;

add_subtopics.title: Self-joins, full outer joins and set operations
add_subtopics.body:
A few more join shapes cover most remaining questions.

FULL OUTER JOIN keeps every row from both sides, with NULLs where one side has no match. It is the tool for reconciling two sources, such as the CRM and the billing system: one query shows rows missing on the left, rows missing on the right, and rows that match but disagree. COALESCE the two keys so every row has an id to show.

A self-join joins a table to itself under two aliases. It answers questions that compare rows in the same table: each employee next to their manager, or each order next to the same customer's previous order.

CROSS JOIN pairs every row of A with every row of B, so 3 stores and 30 days give 90 rows. It sounds useless but builds grids and date spines: a full list of days to LEFT JOIN your data onto, so days with no sales show 0 instead of disappearing from a chart. In PostgreSQL, generate_series makes the list of days.

Set operations stack results vertically instead of side by side. UNION ALL keeps every row. UNION also removes duplicates, which costs a sort or hash and can hide real duplicates you wanted to see, so use UNION ALL unless you need the removal. EXCEPT returns rows in the first query but not the second; INTERSECT returns rows in both. The columns must match in number and type.
add_subtopics.example: A subscription business says finance and the CRM disagree by $41,000. A FULL OUTER JOIN on invoice_id finds 212 invoices only in billing (created by a manual process) and 37 with different amounts (discounts applied after sync). The FDE sends the three lists to the two teams instead of one confusing total.
add_subtopics.code:
CREATE TABLE crm_invoices     (invoice_id text, amount numeric);
CREATE TABLE billing_invoices (invoice_id text, amount numeric);
INSERT INTO crm_invoices     VALUES ('INV-1',100),('INV-2',250),('INV-3',75);
INSERT INTO billing_invoices VALUES ('INV-1',100),('INV-2',240),('INV-4',30);

-- Reconcile two sources: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps rows missing on either side
SELECT COALESCE(c.invoice_id, b.invoice_id) AS invoice_id,
       c.amount AS crm_amount,
       b.amount AS billing_amount,
       CASE WHEN c.invoice_id IS NULL THEN 'missing in CRM'
            WHEN b.invoice_id IS NULL THEN 'missing in billing'
            WHEN c.amount <> b.amount THEN 'amount differs'
            ELSE 'ok' END AS status
FROM   crm_invoices c
FULL OUTER JOIN billing_invoices b ON b.invoice_id = c.invoice_id
ORDER  BY 1;
-- INV-1 | 100 | 100 | ok
-- INV-2 | 250 | 240 | amount differs
-- INV-3 |  75 |     | missing in billing
-- INV-4 |     |  30 | missing in CRM

-- Self-join: each employee next to their manager (same table twice)
CREATE TABLE staff (id int, name text, manager_id int);
INSERT INTO staff VALUES (1,'Priya',NULL),(2,'Tomas',1),(3,'Wen',1),(4,'Kofi',2);
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM   staff e
LEFT JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id
ORDER  BY e.id;
-- Priya | (none)
-- Tomas | Priya
-- Wen   | Priya
-- Kofi  | Tomas

-- CROSS JOIN a date spine: one row per day, even days with no sales
CREATE TABLE sales (sold_on date, amount numeric);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('2026-09-01',50),('2026-09-01',20),('2026-09-03',40);
SELECT d::date AS day, COALESCE(SUM(s.amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM   generate_series(DATE '2026-09-01', DATE '2026-09-04', INTERVAL '1 day') AS d
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.sold_on = d::date
GROUP  BY d
ORDER  BY d;
-- 2026-09-01 | 70
-- 2026-09-02 |  0
-- 2026-09-03 | 40
-- 2026-09-04 |  0

-- CROSS JOIN: every store with every day (a grid to fill in)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS grid_rows
FROM   (VALUES ('north'),('south'),('east')) AS stores(store)
CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 30) AS day;
-- 90

-- UNION removes duplicates (and sorts or hashes to do it); UNION ALL keeps every row
SELECT COUNT(*) AS union_rows FROM (
  SELECT invoice_id FROM crm_invoices UNION     SELECT invoice_id FROM billing_invoices) t;   -- 4
SELECT COUNT(*) AS union_all_rows FROM (
  SELECT invoice_id FROM crm_invoices UNION ALL SELECT invoice_id FROM billing_invoices) t;   -- 6
-- EXCEPT and INTERSECT: in one list but not the other, or in both
SELECT invoice_id FROM crm_invoices EXCEPT SELECT invoice_id FROM billing_invoices;
-- INV-3

add_subtopics.title: Conditional logic, dates and types
add_subtopics.body:
Business rules turn into CASE WHEN. It works like if and else inside a query: CASE WHEN condition THEN value WHEN other_condition THEN value ELSE default END. Conditions are checked top to bottom and the first true one wins, so put the most specific first.

Conditional aggregation puts CASE inside an aggregate to count several things in one pass: SUM(CASE WHEN priority = 'high' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). PostgreSQL and some others also allow COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE priority = 'high'), which is shorter. This replaces running one query per category.

Dividing two integers gives an integer in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite: 3 / 4 is 0, not 0.75. That is why this lesson writes 100.0 * x / y. Multiplying by a decimal or using CAST(x AS numeric) makes the result a decimal. Protect against dividing by zero with NULLIF(y, 0), which turns 0 into NULL, so the result is NULL instead of an error.

For dates, DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) rounds a timestamp down to the start of its month, day or hour, which makes grouping by period easy. With timestamptz (a timestamp with time zone), the time zone decides which day a moment belongs to. An order at 01:30 UTC on 2 September is still 1 September in New York, so a daily report grouped in UTC can disagree with the customer's own report. Agree the reporting time zone and convert with AT TIME ZONE before truncating.

CAST (or :: in PostgreSQL) converts text to numbers or dates, and fails loudly on bad values, which is what you want.
add_subtopics.example: A support team's SLA report shows 91 percent within 4 hours, but their manager counts 87. The FDE finds two causes: tickets opened in the evening in the US were grouped into the next UTC day, and an integer division rounded one team's rate. Converting to America/New_York before DATE_TRUNC and writing 100.0 * fixes both.
add_subtopics.code:
CREATE TABLE tickets (id int, priority text, status text,
                      opened_at timestamptz, resolved_at timestamptz);
INSERT INTO tickets VALUES
 (1,'high','closed','2026-09-01 07:30+00','2026-09-01 09:30+00'),
 (2,'low', 'open',  '2026-09-02 01:30+00',NULL),
 (3,'high','closed','2026-09-02 10:00+00','2026-09-03 10:00+00'),
 (4,'low', 'closed','2026-09-02 12:00+00','2026-09-02 13:00+00');

-- CASE WHEN: label each row
SELECT id,
       CASE WHEN resolved_at IS NULL                        THEN 'open'
            WHEN resolved_at - opened_at <= INTERVAL '4 hours' THEN 'within SLA'
            ELSE 'late' END AS sla
FROM   tickets ORDER BY id;
-- 1 within SLA | 2 open | 3 late | 4 within SLA

-- Conditional aggregation: several counts in one pass
SELECT COUNT(*)                                          AS total,
       SUM(CASE WHEN priority = 'high' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS high_case,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE priority = 'high')          AS high_filter,   -- PostgreSQL
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'open')            AS still_open
FROM   tickets;
-- total 4 | high_case 2 | high_filter 2 | still_open 1

-- Integer division: 3 / 4 is 0 in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite
SELECT 3 / 4 AS int_div, 3 / 4.0 AS decimal_div,
       CAST(3 AS numeric) / 4 AS cast_div, ROUND(100.0 * 3 / 4, 1) AS pct;
-- int_div 0 | decimal_div 0.75000... | cast_div 0.75000... | pct 75.0

-- NULLIF: avoid "division by zero" by turning 0 into NULL
SELECT priority,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'closed') AS closed,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'closed')
             / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 1) AS closed_pct
FROM   tickets GROUP BY priority ORDER BY priority;
-- high | 2 | 100.0
-- low  | 1 |  50.0

-- Dates: DATE_TRUNC buckets timestamps; the time zone decides which day a row lands on
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', opened_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date              AS day_utc,
       DATE_TRUNC('day', opened_at AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York')::date AS day_new_york,
       id
FROM   tickets ORDER BY id;
-- 2026-09-01 | 2026-09-01 | 1
-- 2026-09-02 | 2026-09-01 | 2   <- 01:30 UTC is still 1 September in New York
-- 2026-09-02 | 2026-09-02 | 3
-- 2026-09-02 | 2026-09-02 | 4

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', opened_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS opened
FROM   tickets GROUP BY 1;
-- 2026-09-01 | 4

-- CAST text to numbers and dates (fails loudly on bad input)
SELECT CAST('42.50' AS numeric) + 1 AS n, '2026-09-30'::date + 1 AS next_day;
-- 43.50 | 2026-10-01

replace_subtopics.title: Window functions
replace_subtopics.body:
A window function computes a value across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them. GROUP BY turns many rows into one. A window keeps every row and adds a column.

The syntax is FUNCTION() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...). PARTITION BY splits rows into groups. ORDER BY sets the order within each group. Useful functions include ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG (the previous row's value) and SUM as a running total.

Window functions run at the SELECT step, so to filter on their result, wrap the query in a CTE and filter in the outer query.

ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK differ only when there are ties. For deals of 9, 7, 7 and 5, ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3, 4 (always unique, so ties are broken arbitrarily unless you add a tie-breaker), RANK gives 1, 2, 2, 4 (tied rows share a rank and the next rank is skipped), and DENSE_RANK gives 1, 2, 2, 3 (no gap). Use ROW_NUMBER to pick exactly one row, RANK or DENSE_RANK to return every tied winner.

A frame limits which rows of the window a function sees. ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW means this row and the 6 before it, which gives a 7-day moving average when there is one row per day. The first six rows have fewer days in the window, so show that count or skip them. If some days are missing, build a date spine first, or the frame will span more than 7 calendar days.

The default frame catches people out. With ORDER BY in the OVER clause, the default frame runs from the first row to the current row. That is why SUM gives a running total, and also why LAST_VALUE returns the current row instead of the last one. Write the frame explicitly: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

Keeping one latest row per key is such a common use of ROW_NUMBER that it has its own subtopic in this lesson, along with the QUALIFY shortcut.
replace_subtopics.example: A subscription company wants each customer's most recent plan change and how much their monthly price moved. ROW_NUMBER picks the latest change per customer. LAG gets the previous price so the query can compute the difference, for example from $49 to $99, a change of +$50. The same company's sales dashboard shows a 7-day moving average of new subscriptions using a ROWS frame, and a leaderboard using DENSE_RANK so two reps tied for second both show as 2.
replace_subtopics.code:
WITH changes AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         changed_at,
         monthly_price,
         LAG(monthly_price) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                                  ORDER BY changed_at)        AS prev_price,
         ROW_NUMBER()       OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                                  ORDER BY changed_at DESC)   AS rn
  FROM   plan_changes
)
SELECT customer_id,
       changed_at,
       prev_price,
       monthly_price,
       monthly_price - prev_price AS delta
FROM   changes
WHERE  rn = 1;             -- latest change only; filtering happens outside the window


CREATE TABLE sales_reps (rep text, deals int);
INSERT INTO sales_reps VALUES ('Ana',9),('Ben',7),('Chen',7),('Dara',5);

-- Same tied data, three ranking functions
SELECT rep, deals,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY deals DESC, rep) AS row_number,  -- 1,2,3,4: always unique
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY deals DESC)      AS rank,        -- 1,2,2,4: gap after a tie
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY deals DESC)      AS dense_rank   -- 1,2,2,3: no gap
FROM   sales_reps
ORDER  BY deals DESC, rep;
-- Ana  | 9 | 1 | 1 | 1
-- Ben  | 7 | 2 | 2 | 2
-- Chen | 7 | 3 | 2 | 2
-- Dara | 5 | 4 | 4 | 3

-- Frames: a 7-day moving average (this row and the 6 before it)
CREATE TABLE daily_orders (day date, orders int);
INSERT INTO daily_orders
SELECT d::date, 100 + (EXTRACT(day FROM d)::int % 5) * 10
FROM   generate_series(DATE '2026-09-01', DATE '2026-09-10', INTERVAL '1 day') d;

SELECT day, orders,
       ROUND(AVG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day
                               ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS avg_7d,
       COUNT(*)      OVER (ORDER BY day
                           ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)        AS days_in_window
FROM   daily_orders
ORDER  BY day;
-- 2026-09-01 | 110 | 110.0 | 1
-- 2026-09-02 | 120 | 115.0 | 2
-- ...
-- 2026-09-07 | 120 | 118.6 | 7   <- first full 7-day window
-- 2026-09-10 | 100 | 120.0 | 7

-- The LAST_VALUE surprise: with ORDER BY, the default frame ends at the CURRENT row
SELECT day, orders,
       LAST_VALUE(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day)                  AS last_default,
       LAST_VALUE(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_whole
FROM   daily_orders
WHERE  day <= DATE '2026-09-03'
ORDER  BY day;
-- 2026-09-01 | 110 | 110 | 130
-- 2026-09-02 | 120 | 120 | 130
-- 2026-09-03 | 130 | 130 | 130

replace_subtopics.title: CTEs for readable queries
replace_subtopics.body:
A common table expression (CTE) is a named subquery defined with WITH at the top of a query. It lets you build a result in small, readable steps.

Each CTE can refer to the ones before it. You can run each step on its own while debugging, which is useful when a number looks wrong in front of a customer.

In modern PostgreSQL and most warehouses, CTEs are usually optimised like normal subqueries, so readability rarely costs performance.

More precisely: since PostgreSQL 12, a CTE that is referenced once (and has no side effects) is inlined, meaning the planner merges it into the main query, so filters in the outer query can still use indexes inside it. A CTE referenced two or more times is computed once and stored (materialised). You can override this: WITH c AS MATERIALIZED (...) forces storing, which can help when an expensive step is reused; WITH c AS NOT MATERIALIZED (...) forces inlining. Before version 12, every CTE was materialised, which is why older advice says CTEs are slow. Check with EXPLAIN when in doubt.

A recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) walks hierarchies of unknown depth: org charts, bills of materials, folder trees, account parents. It has two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor query that finds the starting rows, such as the top manager, and a recursive query that joins the table to the rows found so far to find the next level. It stops when a step finds no new rows. Add a depth limit in case the data contains a loop, such as two people listed as each other's manager.
replace_subtopics.example: An insurer wants the average days from claim filed to first payment, for claims filed in Q2, by product line. The FDE builds it in three CTEs: Q2 claims, first payment per claim, and the joined result. When the auto line looks odd, they run the second CTE alone and find duplicate payment rows. The insurer also wants claim totals rolled up through its broker hierarchy, which is between 2 and 6 levels deep. A recursive CTE walks from each top-level broker down, carrying a path such as North > Metro > Harbour Street, and the totals are grouped by the top level.
replace_subtopics.code:
WITH q2_claims AS (
  SELECT claim_id, product_line, filed_at
  FROM   claims
  WHERE  filed_at >= DATE '2026-04-01' AND filed_at < DATE '2026-07-01'
),
first_payment AS (
  SELECT claim_id, MIN(paid_at) AS first_paid_at   -- one row per claim
  FROM   payments
  GROUP  BY claim_id
)
SELECT c.product_line,
       COUNT(*)                                        AS claims,
       ROUND(AVG(p.first_paid_at::date - c.filed_at::date), 1) AS avg_days_to_pay
FROM   q2_claims c
JOIN   first_payment p USING (claim_id)
GROUP  BY c.product_line
ORDER  BY avg_days_to_pay DESC;


CREATE TABLE claims (claim_id int PRIMARY KEY, product_line text, filed_at date);
INSERT INTO claims SELECT g, (ARRAY['auto','home','travel'])[1 + g % 3], DATE '2026-01-01' + g % 300
FROM generate_series(1, 100000) g;
ANALYZE claims;

-- Referenced once: PostgreSQL 12+ inlines the CTE, so the filter reaches the index
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
WITH c AS (SELECT * FROM claims)
SELECT * FROM c WHERE claim_id = 42;
-- Index Scan using claims_pkey on claims
--   Index Cond: (claim_id = 42)

-- MATERIALIZED forces it to be computed once and stored first
EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF)
WITH c AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT * FROM claims)
SELECT * FROM c WHERE claim_id = 42;
-- CTE Scan on c
--   Filter: (claim_id = 42)
--   CTE c
--     ->  Seq Scan on claims      <- reads all 100,000 rows

-- Recursive CTE: walk an org chart from the top down
CREATE TABLE staff (id int, name text, manager_id int);
INSERT INTO staff VALUES (1,'Priya',NULL),(2,'Tomas',1),(3,'Wen',1),(4,'Kofi',2),(5,'Lena',4);

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level, name::text AS path
  FROM   staff
  WHERE  manager_id IS NULL                       -- anchor: the top of the tree
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, c.level + 1, c.path || ' > ' || s.name
  FROM   staff s
  JOIN   chain c ON s.manager_id = c.id           -- recursive step: direct reports
  WHERE  c.level < 20                             -- safety stop if the data has a loop
)
SELECT level, name, path FROM chain ORDER BY path;
-- 1 | Priya | Priya
-- 2 | Tomas | Priya > Tomas
-- 3 | Kofi  | Priya > Tomas > Kofi
-- 4 | Lena  | Priya > Tomas > Kofi > Lena
-- 2 | Wen   | Priya > Wen

replace_subtopics.title: Joins and the fan-out trap
replace_subtopics.body:
A join combines rows from two tables where a condition matches. An INNER JOIN keeps only rows with a match on both sides. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills NULL where the right side has no match.

The cardinality of a relationship is how many rows match on each side. If one order has many shipments, joining orders to shipments produces one row per shipment. Summing order amounts after that join counts each order several times. This is called fan-out.

The fix is to aggregate the 'many' side first, down to one row per key, and then join.

When the join condition or filter value comes from Python, such as a region chosen in a web form, never build the SQL string yourself with an f-string or +. If the value contains a quote, it can change the query itself: north' OR '1'='1 turns a filter into "return every row". This is SQL injection, one of the most common security holes. Instead, write a placeholder (%s in psycopg for PostgreSQL, ? in sqlite3) and pass the values separately. The driver sends them as data, so they can never become SQL. For a list of ids, pass a Python list to = ANY(%s). Placeholders work for values only; if a user picks a table or column name, check it against an allowlist.
replace_subtopics.example: An online store reports $2.4M revenue for August, while finance says $1.6M. The query joined orders to shipments, and split shipments meant about a third of orders appeared twice. Aggregating shipments per order first, then joining, returns $1.6M. In the reporting tool, the region filter was later rewritten from an f-string to a %s placeholder after a tester typed a quote into the region box and got every customer back.
replace_subtopics.code:
-- Fan-out bug: orders with 2 shipments are counted twice
SELECT SUM(o.amount)
FROM   orders o
JOIN   shipments s ON s.order_id = o.order_id;

-- Fix: reduce shipments to one row per order first
WITH ship AS (
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS n_shipments, MAX(shipped_at) AS last_shipped
  FROM   shipments
  GROUP  BY order_id
)
SELECT SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM   orders o
LEFT JOIN ship s ON s.order_id = o.order_id     -- keeps unshipped orders too
WHERE  o.created_at >= DATE '2026-08-01'
  AND  o.created_at <  DATE '2026-09-01';

-- From Python (psycopg): pass values as parameters, never in an f-string
/*
import psycopg

conn = psycopg.connect("dbname=shop"   # plus host and user for your database)
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("CREATE TEMP TABLE customers (customer_id int, name text, region text)")
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO customers VALUES (%s, %s, %s)",
                [(1, "Arden Bikes", "north"), (2, "Birchway Cafe", "south")])

region = "north' OR '1'='1"            # what a malicious or careless user might type

# NEVER: an f-string pastes the text into the SQL, so the OR clause runs
cur.execute(f"SELECT name FROM customers WHERE region = '{region}'")
print("f-string:", cur.fetchall())

# ALWAYS: %s placeholder, values passed separately; the driver sends them as data
cur.execute("SELECT name FROM customers WHERE region = %s", (region,))
print("placeholder:", cur.fetchall())

cur.execute("SELECT name FROM customers WHERE region = %s", ("north",))
print("normal use:", cur.fetchall())

# Lists: use = ANY(%s) with a Python list instead of building IN (...) by hand
cur.execute("SELECT name FROM customers WHERE customer_id = ANY(%s) ORDER BY 1", ([1, 2],))
print("any:", cur.fetchall())
# Placeholders are for values only. Table or column names from users need
# an allowlist, or psycopg.sql.Identifier.

# f-string: [('Arden Bikes',), ('Birchway Cafe',)]   <- injection returned everything
# placeholder: []
# normal use: [('Arden Bikes',)]
# any: [('Arden Bikes',), ('Birchway Cafe',)]
*/

add_glossary: Anti-join
A query that returns rows in one table with no matching row in another, for example with NOT EXISTS.
Semi-join
A query that returns rows in one table that have at least one match in another, each once, for example with EXISTS.
Self-join
Joining a table to itself under two aliases to compare rows in the same table.
FULL OUTER JOIN
A join that keeps all rows from both tables, with NULLs where either side has no match.
Date spine
A complete list of dates used as the base of a query so that days with no data still appear.
UNION ALL
Stacks two query results and keeps every row; UNION also removes duplicates.
Conditional aggregation
Using CASE or FILTER inside an aggregate to count or sum several categories in one pass.
Integer division
Dividing two integers, which drops the fraction in many databases, so 3 / 4 is 0.
Window frame
The set of rows around the current row that a window function uses, set with ROWS BETWEEN.
QUALIFY
A clause in Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and DuckDB that filters on a window function result.
Recursive CTE
A WITH RECURSIVE query that repeats a join step to walk a hierarchy such as an org chart.
SQL injection
An attack where input text changes the meaning of a SQL query because it was pasted into the query string.
Parameterised query
A query with placeholders whose values are sent separately, so they are always treated as data.

add_subtopics.title: Statistics and bad row estimates
add_subtopics.body:
Every estimate the planner makes comes from statistics stored in the catalog. ANALYZE (or autovacuum, which runs it for you) samples each column and records how many distinct values it has, the most common values and how often they appear, and a histogram of the rest. From these, the planner guesses how many rows a filter like city = 'Leeds' will return. That guess is the 'rows=' number in EXPLAIN.

Estimates go wrong in three common ways. First, the statistics are stale, for example after a big load or delete, so run ANALYZE. Second, the sample missed a skewed column, so raise the detail with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS 500 and analyze again. Third, two filtered columns are related, such as city and country. The planner assumes columns are independent and multiplies the two selectivities, which makes the estimate far too small. CREATE STATISTICS tells Postgres that the columns move together.

Why it matters: an estimate that is 100 times too low pushes the planner toward a nested loop or an index scan that is fine for 20 rows and terrible for 2,000. When a plan looks wrong, compare 'rows=' with 'actual rows=' first, then fix the estimate before adding indexes.
add_subtopics.example: A freight company filters shipments by city and country. Every city in country0 belongs to it, so the real match for city7 AND country0 is about 2,000 of 200,000 rows. The planner estimated only 223 because it treated the two columns as independent, and it chose a plan built for a tiny result. After CREATE STATISTICS on (city, country) and ANALYZE, the estimate rose to about 1,900, the planner chose a plan suited to the real size, and the query got faster.

add_subtopics.title: Join algorithms and scan nodes
add_subtopics.body:
When a query joins two tables, the planner picks one of three algorithms, and each shows up as a node name in EXPLAIN.

Nested Loop: for each row from the outer input, look up matching rows in the inner input. It is best when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index on the join column. It is the worst choice when both sides are large, because the inner lookup repeats once per outer row (the loops number).

Hash Join: read the smaller table into an in-memory hash table (the Hash node), then stream the bigger table past it and probe. It is the usual winner for large joins on equality, and needs no index. If the hash table does not fit in work_mem it spills to disk in batches, which is slower.

Merge Join: both inputs arrive sorted on the join column, then are walked together like a zipper. It is chosen when the data is already sorted, for example from an index, or when a sort is cheap.

You will also see Bitmap Index Scan followed by Bitmap Heap Scan very often. The index scan collects the matching row locations into a bitmap, then the heap scan reads the table pages in physical order, once each. The planner uses this in the middle ground: too many rows for a plain Index Scan, too few for a Seq Scan. The Recheck Cond line is normal.
add_subtopics.example: A retailer joins 10,000 customers to 200,000 orders. For one customer, the planner uses a Nested Loop: one index lookup on customers, then a Bitmap Heap Scan on that customer's 20 orders. For a report that totals sales by region across all orders, it switches to a Hash Join: the small customers table is hashed and the 200,000 orders stream past it. Forcing a nested loop on the report would mean 200,000 separate lookups.
add_subtopics.code:
-- Small filtered outer side + indexed inner side -> Nested Loop
EXPLAIN SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM   customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE  c.id = 42;
--  Nested Loop
--    -> Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
--    -> Bitmap Heap Scan on orders o
--         -> Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_id_idx

-- Big equality join, no filter -> Hash Join (the small table is hashed)
EXPLAIN SELECT c.region, sum(o.total)
FROM   customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP  BY c.region;
--  Hash Join  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
--    -> Parallel Seq Scan on orders o
--    -> Hash -> Seq Scan on customers c

-- Both sides come out of indexes already sorted -> Merge Join
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY c.id;
--  Merge Join  Merge Cond: (c.id = o.customer_id)

-- Experiment only: switch an algorithm off for this session to compare plans
SET enable_hashjoin = off;
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT c.region, sum(o.total)
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.region;
RESET enable_hashjoin;

add_subtopics.title: Finding slow queries and keeping tables healthy
add_subtopics.body:
You usually do not know which query is slow. The pg_stat_statements extension answers that. It records, for every distinct query shape, how many times it ran and how much total time it used. Sort by total_exec_time, not by the slowest single run: a 20 ms query that runs 5 million times an hour costs more than a 30-second report that runs once. To turn it on, add pg_stat_statements to shared_preload_libraries, restart, and run CREATE EXTENSION. On managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL) this is usually a parameter setting.

auto_explain writes the plan of any query slower than a chosen threshold into the server log, so you can see the plan that ran in production, not one you reproduced.

Postgres never overwrites a row in place. An UPDATE or DELETE leaves the old version behind as a dead tuple. VACUUM marks that space reusable, and autovacuum runs it in the background. A table with heavy updates or a huge delete can bloat: it holds much more space than its live data, and scans get slower. Plain VACUUM makes space reusable but usually does not shrink the file. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and shrinks it, but takes a lock that blocks all access, so it is a maintenance-window tool.

Indexes need care too: check for unused ones, and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY a badly bloated one.
add_subtopics.example: A telecom's dashboard feels slow. The FDE enables pg_stat_statements, waits a day, and sorts by total time. The top query is a tiny lookup that runs 8 million times, each with a Seq Scan, so it uses most of the database's time. One index fixes it. Two weeks later a purge job deletes half of a 200,000-row table. The file stays at 13 MB until VACUUM FULL, run in a maintenance window, shrinks it to about 6.7 MB.

replace_subtopics.title: B-tree indexes and column order
replace_subtopics.body:
A B-tree is a balanced tree that keeps keys in sorted order. Finding a key takes about log(n) steps, so even a billion rows need only a few levels. Because keys are sorted, a B-tree also handles ranges (created_at > X) and ORDER BY.

A composite index covers several columns, such as (customer_id, created_at). It is sorted by the first column, then the second within each first value. Put columns filtered by equality first and range columns after. A query that does not filter on the first column usually cannot use the index efficiently.

Some things prevent index use: wrapping the column in a function, like lower(email), or a pattern that starts with a wildcard, like LIKE '%smith'. An expression index on lower(email) solves the first case.

Four more things matter on a real customer database.

1) Build indexes without blocking. A plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes to the table until it finishes, which on a big live table can mean minutes of failed orders. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds the index while writes continue. It is slower, cannot run inside a transaction block, and if it fails it leaves an INVALID index that you must drop. Dropping has the same option: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Before dropping, check idx_scan in pg_stat_user_indexes over a full business cycle (month-end jobs may be the only user), and keep the CREATE INDEX statement so you can undo it.

2) A covering index adds extra columns with INCLUDE. If every column the query needs is in the index, Postgres can answer from the index alone (an Index Only Scan) and skip the table. This works best on tables that are vacuumed regularly.

3) A partial index covers only some rows, such as WHERE status = 'open'. It is tiny and fast when queries only care about that slice.

4) Watch for silent index killers. If the column type and the compared value differ, the database may convert the column instead of the value, and an index on the column stops helping. In Postgres, comparing an integer column with a numeric value like 500.0 does this. (Comparing a text column with a bare integer is an error in Postgres, but SQL Server and MySQL convert silently and then scan.) Also, LIKE 'abc%' can only use a plain B-tree index if the database uses the C collation. Otherwise create the index with text_pattern_ops.
replace_subtopics.example: A bank's statement page runs WHERE account_id = 5521 AND posted_at >= '2026-06-01' ORDER BY posted_at DESC LIMIT 50. With an index on (account_id, posted_at), the database jumps to account 5521, walks backward through dates and stops after 50 rows. With the index in the reverse order, it would scan every account's recent rows. Later the same bank adds a nightly job that only reads open disputes. A partial index on (account_id) WHERE status = 'open' is a small fraction of the size of a full one, and the FDE builds it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so customers can keep posting payments during the build.
replace_subtopics.code:
-- Equality column first, range/sort column second
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_account_posted
    ON transactions (account_id, posted_at);

-- Uses the index for the filter AND the sort, stops at 50 rows
SELECT *
FROM   transactions
WHERE  account_id = 5521
  AND  posted_at >= DATE '2026-06-01'
ORDER  BY posted_at DESC
LIMIT  50;

-- Function on the column hides it from a plain index...
-- WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'
-- ...so index the expression instead
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower ON users (lower(email));

-- Build on a live table without blocking writes (not inside BEGIN/COMMIT)
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_txn_disputes_open
    ON transactions (account_id) WHERE status = 'open';   -- also a partial index

-- Check it is valid; a failed concurrent build leaves indisvalid = false
SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index_name, indisvalid
FROM   pg_index
WHERE  indrelid = 'transactions'::regclass;

-- Covering index: INCLUDE columns are stored but not searched
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_cover ON transactions (account_id) INCLUDE (amount);
-- SELECT amount FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 5521;  -> Index Only Scan

-- Drop an unused index without blocking
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_txn_cover;

-- Type mismatch: id is an integer column, 500.0 is numeric
-- EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM shipments WHERE id = 500.0;   -> Seq Scan, Filter: ((id)::numeric = 500.0)
-- EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM shipments WHERE id = 500;     -> Index Scan using shipments_pkey

-- Prefix search on a text column: needs text_pattern_ops unless the C collation is used
CREATE INDEX idx_ship_ref_like ON shipments (ref text_pattern_ops);
-- WHERE ref LIKE '1234%'  -> Index Scan using idx_ship_ref_like

replace_subtopics.title: Partitioning large tables
replace_subtopics.body:
Partitioning splits one logical table into several physical tables based on a key, most often a date range. Queries still address the parent table.

When a query filters on the partition key, the planner skips partitions that cannot contain matching rows. This is called partition pruning. It works like an index at the level of whole chunks.

Partitioning also makes data retention easy. Deleting a year of data from a normal table is slow and leaves bloat. Dropping or detaching a partition is almost instant.

Snowflake and BigQuery have no B-tree indexes, so the tuning tools are different (see the warehouse concept). The same idea of skipping data still applies. In BigQuery you partition a table by a date column and add clustering columns, and queries that filter on the partition column only read (and are billed for) the matching partitions. In Snowflake, data is stored in small micro-partitions, and a clustering key on a large table keeps similar values together so filters can skip most of them. In both, the habit is the same as in Postgres: filter on the partition or clustering column, and never wrap it in a function that hides it.
replace_subtopics.example: An IoT customer stores 4 billion sensor readings. Queries almost always ask for the last 7 days. The FDE partitions the table by month. A query for the last week touches one or two partitions instead of the entire table, and the retention job drops partitions older than 24 months each month. When the same customer moves its history into BigQuery, the FDE partitions the events table by day and clusters it by sensor_id, and requires a date filter so nobody scans (and pays for) the whole table by accident.

add_glossary: Nested Loop
A join that looks up matching inner rows once for each outer row; best when the outer side is small and the inner side is indexed.
Hash Join
A join that builds an in-memory hash table from the smaller input and probes it with the larger one.
Merge Join
A join that walks two inputs sorted on the join column together, like a zipper.
Bitmap Heap Scan
A scan that reads table pages in order after a Bitmap Index Scan has collected the matching row locations.
Index Only Scan
A scan that answers a query from the index alone without visiting the table.
Covering index
An index that stores extra columns with INCLUDE so common queries need no table visit.
Partial index
An index that covers only rows matching a WHERE condition, so it is small and fast.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
Builds an index without blocking writes; slower, and a failed build leaves an INVALID index to drop.
text_pattern_ops
An index operator class that lets LIKE 'abc%' use a B-tree when the database collation is not C.
pg_stat_statements
A Postgres extension that records call counts and total time for each distinct query shape.
auto_explain
A Postgres module that logs the plans of queries slower than a set threshold.
VACUUM
Marks the space of dead row versions as reusable; VACUUM FULL also shrinks the file but blocks access.
Bloat
Wasted space in a table or index from dead row versions that have not been cleaned up.
Extended statistics
Extra statistics created with CREATE STATISTICS so the planner knows that columns are related.
Clustering key
A Snowflake or BigQuery setting that stores similar values together so filters can skip data.
